Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone attacks this year on Russia overnight on Saturday, hitting a key oil terminal in defiance of US President Donald Trump’s demand it stop hitting Russian energy infrastructure.

There have been growing tensions between Ukraine and the US in recent days, prompting fears in Kyiv it could lose essential support as it approaches another winter under relentless Russian attack.

Trump on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress. President Volodymyr Zelensky later told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the US siding with Russia would be a “historic mistake.”

Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday that he doesn’t want to do anything that will drive Russia away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, adding that he believes “great progress is being made.”

At the same time, he excoriated Zelensky, saying that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote.

Despite this, the Ukrainian president said he spoke to US envoy, Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Sunday as part of “nonstop communication” to work towards to goal of peace.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer,” Zelensky posted on X.

But Ukraine is keeping up long-range strikes into Russia. Russia’s defense ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday over various parts of the country.

One target was the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, according to Russian authorities. The terminal can handle up to 12.5 million tons per year. Ukraine’s Fire Point company, which makes the drones used in the attack, said there was a fire on the terminal’s grounds following the strike.

A logistics centers in St. Petersburg was also attacked, according to Ozon, a Russian distribution company, as well as a data center for the Russian VKontakte social media platform.

One person was killed and five wounded in the attacks, with residential homes damaged as well, according to local authorities.

“They shot one down right above us: there was one bright flash, and it shook us up quite strongly,” a 41-year old resident of St. Petersburg told CNN.

“I heard a roar, got everyone out of their beds, took the cat, and we hid in the bathroom,” another said.

Ukraine’s strikes come amid Zelensky’s deteriorating relationship with Trump, who last week called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace.”

A week ago, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, as the White House tries to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices ahead of crucial midterm elections.

Neither Kyiv nor Moscow acknowledged such an agreement. Ukraine briefly halted such attacks, but has since resumed them — while Russia never stopped pounding Ukraine’s energy plants and cities.

Eleven people were killed and nearly 50 injured across Ukraine in Russian missile and drone attacks in the 24 hours to Sunday morning, according to Ukrainian authorities, including what they called a massive attack on energy facilities in the Odesa region.

“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ​ago, Russia has ​deliberately ‌attacked ​Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors ⁠76 times,” Zelensky ​wrote on X Sunday.

Trump has waived sanctions on imports of Russian diesel and on Friday invoked a waiver exempting Russia from sweeping economic penalties mandated by the US Congress, sparking criticism even from Republicans.

In an interview Sunday with “Meet the Press,” Zelensky said the waiver strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield. He said it was “more support for Russian aggression.”

Zelensky also repeated that the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink system to guide its short-range and battlefield drones was still curtailed.

“It was a message from the American government” to limit the speed at which Ukrainian drones could fly, Zelensky said.

The Trump administration has denied it ordered the service restricted.

Zelensky said that intelligence sharing had been blocked by the US side for three days during ballistic missile attacks but had since been restored. US satellite networks have been critical in providing the Ukrainian military with warnings of incoming missiles.

A Ukrainian source told CNN there was no early warning before a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Sunday. This is the third time in a week there has not been an early warning.

Zelensky was also asked about Trump’s comments that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin and replied it was “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”

Zelensky said he wanted to trust Trump and hoped he would change his attitude to Putin.

Asked if Trump was an ally of Ukraine, Zelensky said: “I hope so.”

Daria Tarasova, Julia Benbrook and Jennifer Hanlser contributed to this report.

By

Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday.
                
                    
                    Alessandra Tarantino/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.

The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.

''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.

The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated.

The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.

A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.

''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated.

"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."

American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.

''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''

Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.

"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.

Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."

"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."

Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

The Nebraska Supreme Court Friday upheld the right of eligible U.S. citizens living abroad to vote in the state, in yet another loss for Republicans seeking to restrict overseas voting.

Affirming a lower court’s August decision, the state Supreme Court ruled 6-1 to keep in place the state law that permits those living abroad to vote in certain circumstances.

Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. He stands stoically onstage, barely moving, as he seemingly effortlessly works through deft guitar solos and lopsided riffs. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.

That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.

While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”

What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.

For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”

The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.

When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”

But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”

Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”

About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. We have amps and you know, just, I think some people are responding to the reality of it. Like they really need something that’s not, you know, computer-generated or something.”

He bemoaned the lack of amps onstage (Mascis plays in front of three full stacks, even in a 280-person-capacity club) and the reliance on high-tech front-of-house setups. “It’s very weird. Now, soundmen create the sound instead of capture the sound,” he said. Of course, his recognition of the visceral power of live music and directly connecting with an audience makes his indifference to AI all the more baffling.

Dinosaur Jr. are currently touring the US behind There Near, which is out now.

Pope Leo announced Oct. 11 he would undergo an operation to remove a “localized nodule,” an irregular lump of tissue, in his lung.

The surgical team confirmed an adenocarcinoma diagnosis — a common type of cancer which originates in the glandular cells — after removing the nodule from the lower lobe of his left lung during the roughly 90-minute operation, the Holy See Press Office stated in a Tuesday press release.

“The discovery of the Pope’s malignant lung tumor was entirely accidental, as unfortunately often happens,” Margaritora told Vatican News. “During routine abdominal examinations, this small spot was found in the chest, at the base of the lung … However, if this small spot had been a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen.”

The survival rate for adenocarcinoma depends on its stage, according to City of Hope, a private, non-profit biomedical research, treatment, and education center headquartered in Duarte, California dedicated to cancer, diabetes, and other life-threatening diseases. If the cancer is limited to the lung, the five-year survival rate is 63%; however, if it spreads to other areas of the body, that rate drops to 7%.

Margaritora told Vatican News that he’s “truly pleased” with the pope’s post-operative recovery.

“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery, as the most motivated people do after this kind of operation,” he said. “As a result, he needed very little assistance from us. His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect.”

Margaritora said that, while Pope Leo still needs ten days to fully recover, there are “no clinical reasons” why he shouldn’t undertake his visit to Latin America scheduled for Nov. 6-17.

“Operating on a pope stirred a deep feeling that I cannot even describe,” Margaritora told the outlet. “Obviously, the person before you is a man – after all, the Pope is a man – but you know very well that he is not an ordinary person. Pope Leo has such charisma that it would be impossible to regard him as ordinary.”

Venezuelan composer Gus Ormo was found “tied up” and submerged at the bottom of his South Florida backyard pool in a death that authorities have called a “suspicious incident.”

Ormo, a piano virtuoso and singer known for his romantic compositions, was pronounced dead at the scene after Broward County Sheriff’s deputies responded to a 911 call at around 9 am, officials said.

Audio from the 911 dispatcher stated that a person called about a man who had been “tied up” and possibly drowned in a pool.

Aerial footage captured by local media outlet WPLG Local 10 showed a long blue cord tangled on the musician’s patio that led into the lavish backyard pool.

Ormo’s sister, Antonieta Ormo, confirmed to CBS News Miami that Ormo had died but said the family has no further information on the circumstances surrounding his death.

Ormo’s death is being investigated by homicide and crime scene unit detectives, Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Gerdy St. Louis told reporters.

The composer’s body was taken to the Broward County Medical Examiner’s Office, where officials are working to determine a cause of death, CBS reported.

Ormo had kept a low profile in the sleepy gated community of Weston, neighbors said, and they were shocked to learn of his grisly death.

“It’s sad what happened, and it wasn’t something I expected to happen in Weston,” neighbor Bruno Gedikinan told NBC 6.

Another neighbor described the incident as something completely beyond the pale for the neighborhood.

“It’s weird to happen. It’s not normal, of course,” Mariano Cascata said.

Ormo was fresh off promoting his latest album AGAPE, a piano instrumental album that was described as a “milestone in his career” in an October press release.

“Gus Ormo has always been a sensitive person. He recalls how, as a child, he would listen to records and feel music stirring his deepest emotions,” the release stated.

“There are no secrets,” writer Nora Ephron once opined. Perhaps she should have added a corollary: “Kennedy secrets always sell books.”

Fresh case in point is “Ladies’ Man: The Careless Heart of John F. Kennedy,” a compendium of the love affairs of the 35th President, beginning when he was 17 and attending Choate, a Connecticut prep school.

Author Laurence Leamer, who previously penned “Capote’s Women,” and “Hitchcock’s Blondes” inevitably goes over old ground in this new book, but the vast number of women and incidents he includes makes “Ladies’ Man,” if not edifying, certainly astonishing for sheer scope. It’s a wonder that Kennedy accomplished as much as he did, so frequently was he jumping in and out of bed.

His secret? Keep the encounters brief, and the affairs — if you want to call them that — short-lived.

Those around Kennedy were aware of his brazen promiscuity, but the general public remained oblivious during his lifetime. He never suffered any consequences for behavior that was not merely unbecoming, but downright scuzzy.

Did Kennedy love any of his paramours? Leamer makes the case that two Scandinavians captured his heart — at least for a time. The first, Inga Arvad, was a sophisticated older woman whom Kennedy met in November 1941 through his sister Kathleen, her colleague at the Washington Times-Herald. Then 24 and a naval ensign, Kennedy fell hard for the 28-year-old Danish journalist, and their letters reveal a passionate and confiding intimacy. “She came to understand him in ways no one else in his life ever had, to see him in all his flawed and fractured glory,” Leamer writes of Arvad. “As for Jack, he opened himself up to Arvad, exposing every emotion and concern.”

Arvad was married, although estranged, from her second husband, movie director Paul Fejos. More problematic were her links to Adolf Hitler, whom she had met and interviewed while working in Berlin. The German leader praised her as the perfect example of Nordic beauty, and Arvad attended parties hosted by high-ranking Nazis. She was even photographed sitting next to Hitler in his box during the 1936 Olympics.

After Pearl Harbor, the FBI began investigating Arvad as a possible spy. That same month Kennedy was transferred to South Carolina, where, unbeknownst to the couple, their hotel meet-ups and telephone calls were recorded by the bureau. Kennedy’s father disapproved of his relationship with a married woman of dodgy reputation, and Arvad was involved with at least one other man, so the couple broke up in March 1942.

Gunilla von Post, a Swedish aristocrat, met then-Senator Kennedy when she and a friend were hitchhiking on the Cote d’Azur in July 1953. An old English friend of Kennedy’s offered them a ride and then, driving a few miles further into Cap d’Antibes, was surprised to spot the senator standing by the side of the road. Kennedy, due to wed Jacqueline Bouvier two months later, was indulging in a last solo jaunt as a bachelor.

The foursome went out for dinner and dancing that evening. Von Post, 21, was enchanted by Kennedy, and how, as the band played “I Love Paris,” he crooned the words into her ear. Later, as they stood on a cliff overlooking the Mediterranean, Kennedy declared: “I fell in love with you tonight.”

Then he confessed he was heading back to America to be married. Von Post allowed Kennedy to walk her home, but when he asked to come in for a nightcap, she sent him away.

For most men, that would be the end of it. Yet Kennedy continued to pursue von Post, writing from his Senate office, asking to see her again. He contrived to travel to Sweden two years later, with friend Torbert Macdonald as beard, to spend a week with his young lover, while wife Jackie, who had nursed him tenderly through back surgery, stayed home. Von Post, later a neighbor of Leamer’s in Palm Beach, told the author that their time together was “one of the few weeks in [Kennedy’s] life that he was free as a bird.”

(Poor Jack…not!)

Von Post’s mother blocked Kennedy’s plan to install her in Manhattan’s Carlyle Hotel where he could drop by regularly. They met once again, by chance, at a banquet at the Waldorf Astoria in 1958. Von Post waited for Jacqueline Onassis to pass away in 1994, before writing and publishing a fond memoir titled “Love, Jack.”

Other young women were treated with far more callousness.

Kennedy picked up Diana de Vegh, then a junior at Radcliffe College, at a campaign fundraising dinner in Boston in 1958. The candidate, prowling the ballroom, spotted her and asked her date to give up his seat “so a tired old man can sit next to a pretty girl.”

De Vegh was flattered by Kennedy’s interest, not anticipating that a couple of weeks later, after she’d accompanied him to other campaign events, he’d take her to his Boston apartment for “quick and efficient” sex.

For several years Kennedy continued to hook up with de Vegh, and arranged a job for her in the White House after he was elected President. He’d hint to her that he’d like to be introduced to some of her friends. She refused that request, but otherwise always came when he called.

“Back then, I thought my job was to become pleasing, an enabling acolyte to a master of the universe,” de Vegh explained to Leamer.

Kennedy dispatched with Mimi Beardsley’s virginity in his wife’s bedroom while ostensibly giving the 19-year-old intern a private tour of the White House in 1962. Beardsley subsequently swam with him the White House pool, stayed overnight when the First Lady was away, and accompanied him on overseas trips. White House staffers recognized the  role this intern with scant secretarial skills was playing in the President’s life, and journalists saw Beardsley slipping out of Air Force One. Even so, the secret of her involvement with the Kennedy held for 40 years.

Only the Katers — Leonard and Florence — made a serious effort to expose Kennedy’s proclivities at the time. The couple, devout Catholics, rented a room in their Georgetown townhouse to Pamela Turnure, who worked as a receptionist in Kennedy’s office. When they realized in 1958 that the senator was making illicit nighttime visits to Turnure, 21, they confronted him, and even snapped a photo of him exiting the house, furious that he was passing himself off to voters as a good Christian. They contacted the FBI, sent letters and the photo to various newspapers to report the affair, and Florence picketed the White House.

Kennedy’s aides, who adored him, worked hard to discredit and sideline the Katers, author Leamer told the Post. “Also, it was a different, more deferential era.” If however, Kennedy had lived to run for re-election in 1964, Leamer believes, his sexual exploits may well have come to light as well as his very poor health.

These two secrets — that Kennedy would try to bed any attractive woman in his orbit, and that he suffered from severe and chronic health problems — were linked. “He never wanted to think of himself as sickly,” Leamer explained. “Sex was a way of expressing his vitality.”

Plus, Kennedy relished the danger that illicit assignations involved. “He was always reckless from the time he was young,” Leamer said. “He got off on taking incredible risks.”

Don’t hibernate just yet.

New Yorkers have one more chance to soak up the crisp fall air before the city turns into a freezer.

Street fairs are taking over neighborhoods across the five boroughs this October and November, bringing food vendors, local businesses, shopping, entertainment and prime people-watching to car-free stretches of NYC.

With fairs continuing into November, there’s still time for one last outdoor shopping spree, snack run or leisurely neighborhood stroll before the puffer coats come out.

So skip the pumpkin patch for a weekend and hit the pavement instead.

The Post rounded up 10 NYC street fairs worth checking out this fall before winter sends everyone back indoors.

The Bronx is kicking off the weekend with the 161st Street Friday Fair, an outdoor community street festival and vendor market near Yankee Stadium.

The Oct. 16 fair will bring arts and crafts vendors, food, entertainment and activities to East 161st Street, giving locals a reason to make a pit stop in the neighborhood — even if they’re not headed to a game.

As seen in videos from previous years on social media, there’ll be gyros, empanadas and funnel cakes to fuel a stroll past the vendors, while balloon-twisting clowns offer entertainment for younger fairgoers.

Shoppers can also browse crystals and other merchandise — because what’s a New York street fair without a little food, fun and spiritual cleansing?

When: Friday, Oct. 16, 11 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: East 161st Street, Grand Concourse to Walton Avenue, the Bronx.

Queens is leaning hard into fall with the Forest Hills Autumn Fair, where shoppers can browse arts and crafts, handmade treasures, antiques, collectibles and other unique wares.

Like last year’s fair, there will also be food vendors, children’s rides, live music, games and activities, making it an easy Sunday outing for anyone not ready to surrender to sweater weather just yet.

The event listing also highlights the fair’s mix of local shopping and family-friendly entertainment.

Expect Queens-themed artwork, fresh Italian sausage, lobster rolls and handmade artisan totes, along with thrifted graphic tees and other one-of-a-kind finds. With both shopping and kid-friendly entertainment, it’s a chance to turn a routine neighborhood stroll into a full afternoon out.

When: Sunday, Oct. 18, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Where: 71st/Continental Avenue, Queens Boulevard to Austin Street, Forest Hills, Queens

Broadway gets a harvest-season makeover for the 31st annual Upper Broadway Harvest Fair.

Come hungry and ready to shop as vendors take over the Upper West Side with food, crafts, merchandise and more.

As shown in clips from the past few years, this fair is always a little bit of everything: handmade crafts and local treasures, collectibles and quirky finds, live music, street-fair food and rides to keep the kids busy.

The long-running neighborhood tradition is also a good excuse to wander around Manhattan Valley and soak up some fall scenery while you’re at it.

When: Sunday, Oct. 25, 10 a.m.–5 p.m.

Where: Broadway, W. 96th to W. 106th streets, Manhattan

Brooklyn is going out with a bang: The Court Street Spectacular is billed as the borough’s “last big street fair of 2026.”

For most of the day on Oct. 25, Court Street will fill with merchants, local skincare and homeware vendors, fried Oreos and kid-friendly amusement rides.

That means parents can browse neighborhood shops and grab a bite while younger fairgoers get their own dose of entertainment.

The free, all-ages annual fair runs between Atlantic Avenue and Joralemon Street, through the heart of the Brooklyn Heights and Cobble Hill area. It’s an easy excuse to browse the neighborhood before Halloween — and perhaps reward yourself with a post-fair bite.

When: Sunday, Oct. 25, 11 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: Court Street, Atlantic Avenue to Joralemon Street, Brooklyn.

Think of this one as a fall shopping spree with a Downtown Brooklyn backdrop.

The Fulton Mall/MetroTech Series Fair takes over Lawrence Street from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with handmade goods, vintage trinkets, collectibles and local merchandise on offer.

There will also be food and live music, making this weekday fair a convenient excuse to break up the workweek with some browsing.

When: Wednesday, Nov. 4, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: Lawrence St., Fulton St. to Willoughby St., Downtown Brooklyn

Take a stroll down Eighth Avenue without having to dodge quite so many cars at the Midtown West Fair, which stretches eight blocks through one of the city’s busiest corridors.

Browse food and merchandise vendors before making a day of it in Hell’s Kitchen and the Theatre District, with Broadway theaters, restaurants and bars all within walking distance.

Because apparently the best way to recover from Times Square chaos is with a street-fair snack.

When: Saturday, Nov. 7.

Where: Eighth Ave., W. 42nd to W. 50th streets, Manhattan

The Union Square Autumn Fair is the perfect excuse to spend a Sunday downtown — and pretend you’re holiday shopping for everyone on your list when you’re really shopping for yourself.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., browse annual vendors along 17th Street selling everything from mini pumpkins and fresh fruit to Latin American barbecue and cozy fall sweaters. Then wander through Union Square’s surrounding shops, restaurants and famous Greenmarket.

The free fair runs rain or shine, so don’t let a little November drizzle rain on your shopping parade.

When: Sunday, Nov. 8, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: 17th St., Broadway to Park Ave. South, Manhattan

Celebrate Veterans Day in Lower Manhattan at this free street festival, where food vendors and market stalls line Broadway from Liberty Street to Battery Place from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The festivities coincide with NYC’s annual Veterans Day Parade, which marches up Fifth Avenue from 26th Street toward Midtown, typically ending between 47th and 50th streets.

After browsing the festival, keep the downtown adventure going with a stroll through the Financial District or along the waterfront at The Battery.

When: Wednesday, Nov. 11, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: Broadway, Liberty St. to Battery Place, Lower Manhattan

The Financial District gets its own fall street-fair moment with the Financial Community Fall Fair on Park Place.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., browse snack and clothing vendors while taking in the neighborhood’s unmistakable skyscraper backdrop.

It’s a particularly easy midday outing for downtown workers — or anyone looking for an excuse to play hooky from the office for a little seasonal shopping.

When: Thursday, Nov. 12, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: Park Place, Broadway to Church St., Lower Manhattan

Give thanks for one more excuse to be outside before the Big Apple turns into a freezer.

This free late-season street fair takes over Sixth Avenue from 23rd to 34th streets, with food and merchandise vendors lining the route through Chelsea, Flatiron and NoMad.

Running from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., it’s a final chance to get your outdoor shopping and snacking fix before winter really sets in — and a good excuse to stroll the neighborhood while you still can without three layers of clothing.

When: Sunday, Nov. 15, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

Where: Sixth Ave., W. 23rd to W. 34th streets, Manhattan

The countdown to winter may be on, but New Yorkers aren’t hibernating just yet.

Whether you’re hunting for handmade goods, grabbing a street-fair snack or simply looking for an excuse to wander a different neighborhood, these fairs offer one more reason to get outside before the gloves, scarves and SAD lamps take over.

After all, in The City That Never Sleeps, you don’t need much of an excuse to eat something delicious on a closed-off street.

After you win the economics Nobel, what would your first act be? Buy a Corvette? Gloat to your childhood bully? For co-winner Michael Woodford, his first act was … proctor an exam. The DAY that Columbia professor Michael Woodford found out that he and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel, he returned to his class with the pithy title "Cognitive Mechanisms and Economic Behavior" to administer an exam. He was welcomed to the classroom with cheers and applause. He held up his arms in triumph.

Michael Woodford, Columbia University professor and winner of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.

Coming up:

What to know: Character.ai is a company that allows you to speak with a "companion" — an AI-powered fictional character, historical figure, or whatever you decide to build. It came out just before ChatGPT and quickly went viral in part thanks to its adoption on TikTok. It hit 28 million monthly active users at its peak.

Character.ai had a lot of engagement, a big customer base, lots of talent … and Google promptly picked 'em up for $2.7 billion back in 2024. But Google didn't buy the company and absorb it! No, that traditional "acquihire" model would require all sorts of legal and regulatory approvals. Instead, they hired away the founders (and other big hitters on the team) and bought the nonexclusive license to the technology, leaving the company itself behind. That's called a "reverse acquihire," and it's happened at least six times in the past two years with AI startups. Now this week, Character.ai is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

Some of the "Characters" available to users
                
                    
                    Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Why it matters: A "reverse acquihire" doesn't leave a company in the greatest position. After the Google deal, Character.ai had to change its business model away from the quite costly LLM training and toward developing AI characters. Its founders were gone. Sure, the shrunken company had $2.7 billion in the bank, but leadership was still looking to raise money as they struggled to monetize their user base.

So is the "reverse acquihire" what caused the pain? Or was it a symptom of a larger issue? Character.ai faced a mountain of litigation over alleged harm to minors plus copyright concerns from Disney. So what's left behind? A once very promising company, which Disney is very excited to pick over for parts of it for $20 million.

What's going on: President Trump signed a deal last week to get diesel from Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Two weeks ago, we talked in the newsletter about the potential of a diesel export ban to lower prices. It didn't happen. One week ago, we talked again about Trump issuing an executive order to defer a tax from diesel. Now, this!

It's safe to say people were surprised by the move, given Trump signed a Russian sanctions law just last month that looked to tamp down on their energy revenues. Beyond surprise, a bipartisan group of senators is openly calling for the president to rescind the deal. They said it gives Putin the funds to power his war machine and "enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

Will this do anything? The same bipartisan group of senators said this deal will mean "limited to no relief to Americans." Goldman Sachs estimated the release of Russian oil would affect wholesale prices by $1 to $2 per barrel. The price of a barrel of diesel is around $200. So a $1 to $2 impact? Neil Atkinson, an independent energy analyst, says, "Frankly, [it's] a rounding error. It makes no fundamental difference to the global diesel market."

What's weirder to Atkinson, though … Russia hasn't really been exporting diesel. Its refineries have been damaged, and it's literally been importing diesel to make up for shortfalls. " So where these barrels of Russian diesel are going to come from to go either to the United States or elsewhere in the global market is a bit of a mystery," said Atkinson.

If you HAVEN'T listened: Reporter Greg Rosalsky opens the piece describing WHAT exactly Michael Woodford and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel for. They helped shape what's known as NEW Keynesian economics by bringing microeconomic principles to the traditional models of John Maynard Keynes. BUT THEN, Greg goes on to explain that the Nobel Prize did not initially include an economics award. No, that changed when the Swedish Central Bank, the oldest central bank in the world, wanted to celebrate its 300th anniversary with a bang. They would fund a new award for economics. It's a fascinating story which you can listen to below.

If you HAVE listened: A leading philosophy of John Maynard Keynes is that governments could fight recessions by boosting spending, and deal with inflation by holding spending back. In the initial draft that didn't make it into the final episode, Greg touched on how STAGFLATION was a central thorn in the side of this concept. Specifically, back in the 1970s, during the Arab oil embargo, the U.S. dealt with the one-two punch of high unemployment and high inflation, bringing about stagflation. It challenged the Keynesian idea that when lots of people are out of work and spending less, inflation comes down. Because at that point, unemployment and inflation rose together. Isn't that nice? Greg Rosalsky writes Planet Money's newsletter … you can catch that here.

Rest of the week

Producer Cooper Katz McKim is reading The AGI Chronicles

Man oh man, this is the page-turniest nonfiction book I've read in a while. Kevin Roose, co-host of the upcoming NPR podcast Machine Gods, formerly The New York Times' Hard Fork, tracks the handful of characters racing to make AI a commercial reality. It is far from a clear-cut story. There's no one character who came up with the idea and executed it … the existence of AI today comes down to many papers, many individual discoveries, and a whole lot of obsession. I didn't realize how much progress had been made in AI prior to 2020 and how concerned many industry leaders were about even creating AI (looking at you, Amodei) for fear of creating a super-intelligence that moves outside of human control. It's gossip-y, it's matter of fact … I would recommend.

ice-detainee-property-lawsuit:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent stands outside of immigration court hearings, at Jacob K. Javits Federal Building on June 10, 2025, in New York City.Adam Gray/Getty

Seven people detained previously by ICE filed a lawsuit on Tuesday against the agency, accusing it of illegally refusing to return their personal documents and belongings months after they were released from custody.

Items allegedly withheld include Social Security cards, employment authorization documents, and phones, which the seven individuals allege is a violation of the Fourth Amendment—and ICE’s own confiscation directive, which only permits officers to keep belongings for a clearly defined reason, such as relation to a criminal case.

The ACLU of the District of Columbia, one of the bodies representing the seven plaintiffs, pointed in part to a 2024 federal appeals court ruling in Washington, DC, that barred that city’s police from holding personal property they seize for what the court deemed an unreasonable length of time.

Withholding items like employment documents prevents immigrants from being able to keep their jobs, the suit contends—at least some of the plaintiffs attest that they have indeed lost their jobs—and makes them fear leaving their homes due to lack of documentation.

One plaintiff from Russia with a pending asylum case, Vladimir Izmailov, was “unable to get meaningful employment without his work authorization documents,” ACLU of DC wrote—the suit details that ICE hasn’t returned these documents, and other items including his wedding ring, for more than five months.

“Now, I’m struggling to provide for my family because ICE still has my documents that show I am authorized to work,” Izmailov stated; he said that he has been forced to borrow money to make rent and continue to house himself, his wife, and their two children.

The lawsuit comes following a series of reports of similar incidents. My colleague Julia Lurie wrote about cases in Minnesota in February: “It’s more the rule than the exception that people generally are not given their stuff back,” Graham Ojala-Barbour, a Minneapolis immigration attorney, said in an interview for that article. “As far as I can tell, it’s the practice of ICE to throw everybody’s documents into a black box and then lose it.”

As she reported at the time:

Federal law requires noncitizens to carry proof of their lawful status. “The government not returning these documents to folks is essentially forcing them to walk around without this document that the government itself says these folks are supposed to carry with them,” says Julia Decker, policy director of the Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to order ICE to return their items—and to stop the agency from continuing to unlawfully retain property without just reason.

By DAVID BARRETT, HOME AFFAIRS EDITOR

Published:  04:55 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  06:46 AEDT, 16 October 2026

The mother of Henry Nowak's killer, who was jailed for removing the murder weapon from the scene, is to be freed after serving just one-third of her sentence thanks to Labour's early release scheme.

Kiran Kaur, 53, is due to be let out of jail early in December under a controversial programme that plans to free up to 50,000 offenders a year.

She was jailed for three years on July 17 after being convicted of assisting an offender, her son Vickrum Digwa – who stabbed 18-year-old Mr Nowak to death in Southampton with an eight-inch ceremonial dagger on December 3 last year.

Kaur will be one of the most high-profile criminals to benefit from Labour's soft justice programme so far.

It is thought she had spent about seven months in prison on remand before her sentencing, meaning she will be eligible for release in December after completing one-third of her punishment.

Her son was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 21 years in June.

Digwa, a Sikh, did not know his teenage victim but lied to police officers at the scene by claiming Mr Nowak shouted racist abuse, punched him and knocked off his turban.

Kiran Kaur, 53, was found guilty at Southampton Crown Court earlier this year of assisting an offender by removing a weapon from the scene of the murder of Henry Nowak

Henry Nowak, 18, was murdered in Southampton last December by Vickrum Digwa, 23, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused by his victim

The murder weapon used by Digwa, an eight-inch Sikh kirpan ceremonial knife

Digwa, pictured, was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 21 years in June

Mr Nowak was then arrested as he lay covered in his own blood, before dying alone in police custody.

Following Digwa and his mother's sentencings, the Crown Prosecution Service released footage of the moment the murderer told her to take the knife he had used to kill Mr Nowak.

In the video, Digwa could be heard talking to his mother in Punjabi asking her to take away the weapon. The clip was taken on Digwa's phone and was pointed to the ground.

A transcript released by the CPS revealed how Digwa told Kaur: 'Take this', which prosecutors said was referring to the knife.

During her sentencing at Southampton Crown Court Judge William Mousley said when Digwa told Kaur to take the murder weapon away 'by then you knew or believed that he had stabbed and injured Henry'.

The judge also told Kaur: 'A responsible parent would have challenged their son over their actions and encourage them to do the right thing.'

Kaur took the murder weapon home and put it with a 'larger collection of ceremonial and other weapons in your son's bedroom', Judge Mousley said.

He added that this would have helped to conceal its use because she wanted him to 'avoid being caught'.

The judge said her actions 'added to your son's pretence that he had done nothing wrong and that he was the victim', and added that she added to the 'degradation of Henry being arrested when he was dying'.

Prosecuting barrister Nicholas Lobbenberg told the court that the weapon was not found by police until December 10 last year – seven days after the attack.

It remains unclear whether Kaur, an Indian national, will face deportation proceedings, according to ITV News, which first reported Kaur's impending release.

A Home Office spokesman said: 'Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Henry Nowak, whose life was cruelly cut short in a horrific act of violence.

'We will always seek to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity.'

Labour's prison release scheme launched at the start of this month.

From November 10 it will be extended to offenders serving sentences up to three years and three months, meaning Kaur will become eligible.

Labour's new programme is broader in scope than its previous release scheme, launched in 2024, which saw 70,000 criminals let out early in its first 19 months.

Despite being scheduled for early release, Kaur will appeal against her sentence at the Court of Appeal on November 5.

On the same day the court is due to consider an appeal by Digwa against his sentence, and also decide on a referral from the Attorney General which argued the sentence was too lenient. Digwa is also mounting a separate appeal against his conviction.

By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR

Published:  06:39 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  07:59 AEDT, 16 October 2026

The King and Queen ignored a small but loud group of protestors as they opened the Welsh parliament today.

The couple also put the noise of Nottingham, where Harry and Meghan were on manoeuvres, to one side as they had a poignant meeting with a survivor of the Aberfan disaster and the great-grandson of the school caretaker who saved his life.

Charles clasped the hand of Gareth Jones, 66, who was overcome with emotion as he spoke to the monarch at the Senedd building in Cardiff, showing him a photograph of himself as a child with Prince Philip, a day after Pantglas junior school was engulfed by slurry 60 years ago.

Heavy rain caused a colliery tip on the mountain to collapse and fall onto the school, killing 144 people, including 116 children.

'How are you keeping?' asked the King, with concern. 'We are coming soon, for the commemoration.'

Gareth was just six years old when his teacher pushed him through the classroom window and the school caretaker Stephen Andrew pulled him to safety, telling him, 'Run boy, run home.'

Stephen's great-grandsons Noah Jones, 10, and his brother Charlie, nine, were alongside him to present a posy to the Queen.

Noah met Gareth by chance when he came to give a talk at his school and described being rescued by the school caretaker, not knowing that his descendant was sitting in front of him.

King Charles III and Queen Camilla arrive to attend the ceremonial opening of the Senedd in Cardiff

As they arrived in Cardiff Bay, they were met with a small but protest from demonstrators carrying yellow 'Not My King' placards and shouting the same, along with 'Down with the crown

Charles met with Gareth Jones, 66, who showed him a photograph of himself as a child with Prince Philip, a day after Pantglas junior school was engulfed by slurry 60 years ago

Between them was the framed photograph of the late Duke of Edinburgh speaking to Gareth's family as the little boy looked on, a day after the disaster. The King peered closely at it before smiling and saying 'I recognise him!'

The royal couple were also introduced to Len Moss, an off-duty nurse who rushed to the scene at Pantglas school and spent two days washing the faces and hands of children pulled from the rubble so they could be identified by their loved ones.

The King and Queen were in Cardiff to attend the opening of the Welsh Parliament, with Charles taking part in the ceremony for the first time as monarch.

As they arrived in Cardiff Bay, they were met with a small but protest from demonstrators carrying yellow 'Not My King' placards and shouting the same, along with 'Down with the crown.'

But the welcome was otherwise warm. They were greeted by First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth and the Llywydd (presiding officer) Huw Irranca-Davies, and introduced to the Welsh leaders of Plaid Cymru, Labour, Reform, the Conservative Party and the Liberal Democrats.

After making their way past representatives of the King's Trust, Cardiff's Chinese Community, Learning Disability Wales and Welsh Women's Aid, they walked in procession behind Mace bearer Delyth Lewis - the first woman to hold the role - into the Siambr.

Inside the refurbished circular chamber, the King addressed the newly expanded assembly, made up of 96 members, in English and Welsh.

Paying tribute to the people of Aberfan, he said: 'The Welsh people, from all communities and faiths, are rightly famed for the strength of their sense of belonging – and next week, together with The Queen and The Prince of Wales, I will be visiting Aberfan to commemorate the solemn anniversary of a tragedy that brought Wales to the attention, and to the hearts, of the entire world – for the most unbearable of reasons.

'I am enormously touched that people from the Aberfan community are with us today. There could be no finer witnesses to the strength of the Welsh – and the human – spirit'

Charles and Camilla will visit the community with Prince William on October 21, exactly 60 years after the disaster.

Elsewhere, there was laughter as he cited the title of a famous Welsh protest song Yma o Hyd, now adopted as the anthem of the Welsh football team, saying of the expanded Senedd: 'There are many new faces – as well, of course, as the reassuring presence of familiar faces who are, we might say, Yma o Hyd [still here].

He ended his speech to applause, saying: 'Pob bendith ar eich gwaith er lles y wlad arbennig hon. [Heartfelt thanks for your work for the welfare and success of this special land.]'

Speaking afterwards Noah, from Troedyrhiw, the next village along from Aberfan, said he was, 'Excited, nervous, but happy,' to meet the King and Queen.

Charles and Camilla meet members of the public after attending the ceremonial opening of the Senedd in Cardiff

Charles and Camilla arrive to attend the Ceremonial Opening of the Seventh Senedd

School children wave flags as they wait for the arrival of Charles and Camilla in Cardiff

The Sussexes made their first UK appearance after four years during a series of royal-style engagements in Nottingham today

Their mother Gemma Bray said of the King: 'He said how handsome they both were. And he said how proud you must be.' She said the Queen told the boys, 'You look like twins. And she said that she has twins in her family. And they always fight!'

Gareth, who will be reunited with the King and Queen at next week's commemoration events in Aberfan, said: 'Today has been absolutely emotional, but it's been an amazing day for me.'

Recalling his meeting with Prince Philip back in 1966, he said: 'He actually shot down to Aberfan to visit the day after the disaster. Our house got wrecked, really all water, flood water. So we had to go a few days down with my grandma and grandpa.

Philip was walking down the street when he spotted Gareth and his older siblings sitting on the front wall and came straight over.

'I'm convinced he stopped because there were children there. There were no other children there because unfortunately they were never to return home,' said Gareth.

The late Queen Elizabeth II famously delayed visiting Aberfan in the wake of the tragedy, not wanting to disrupt the rescue operation, a decision which prompted criticism at the time.

'The Queen came about a week later,' recalls Gareth. 'When she came to Aberfan, everybody welcomed her with open arms, and she kept a promise that day that [she would] always come back to Aberfan and keep in contact, and she did.

'Charles has stepped now into her shoes. William is going to be our next king. He then will step into his shoes and will probably contact people in Aberfan and keep it going.'

WASHINGTON — Ukrainian officials were enraged Wednesday after Elon Musk’s SpaceX limited Kyiv’s access to its Starlink satellite service without warning, disrupting combat drone operations while Russian forces launched a fresh round of attacks on civilian targets.

The throttling capped the velocity of Ukrainian drones at 100 miles per hour, with a source familiar with the situation telling The Post: “This makes the operation of UAVs, airplanes, and helicopters at high speeds impossible, which will also impact efforts to counter [Russian] Shahed drones within Ukraine.

“It will affect our defense operations, logistics, etc., mid-strikes,” the person added. “This will also give Russians a real leverage on a front line at the time when we effectively stopped their advances, and de-occupy the territories.”

“Our defense forces did not receive ​a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of ⁠several missions,” presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov complained on Telegram.

Ukraine’s military has long relied on Starlink access — for which Poland pays some $50 million per year — to defend its territory against Russian strikes.

Separately, President Trump has repeatedly pressured Kyiv to stop striking Russian energy targets, for which Ukraine uses separate technology, citing spiking global energy prices.

Following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, Trump announced a deal to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Moscow’s diesel to ease prices at home.

Trump also blasted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and suggested that his countrymen should select a new leader. SpaceX boss Elon Musk later echoed those sentiments, posting on X Saturday that “Zelensky has gone too far.”

“I agree, time for Ukraine to get a new leader,” he added Sunday.

The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, uses the same technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light which scooped the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. Source: The Guardian

Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children. The death toll in Florida from Hurricane Isaias has risen to six, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced during a news conference Tuesday.

The updated storm-related death toll follows reports of two additional deaths: a woman who was killed when a tree fell on her home in Escambia County and a man who died from carbon monoxide poisoning after improperly using a generator.

Gov. DeSantis said the newly announced deaths occurred “a little bit more post-storm” and were “attenuated from the storm.”

“The way Florida has typically done this is it’s not just if the storm knocks over your house and somebody gets killed, they kind of link anything that is even a fallout of the storm,” Gov. DeSantis said.

Gov. DeSantis described the four storm-related deaths as a “tragic accident” involving a falling tree during cleanup, one death in a car accident and two deaths resulting from disruptions to medical treatment.

The grim update comes as recovery efforts continue across a concentrated area of northwest Florida, days after the dangerous Category 2 hurricane made landfall near Destin on the Gulf Coast around 9:30 p.m. ET Friday.

Two additional storm-related deaths were reported in Alabama, including one person who was killed when a tree fell onto a Birmingham home.

Details surrounding the second death were not immediately available.

Florida bore the brunt of Isaias’ worst landfall impacts, with destructive wind gusts reaching 118 mph, heavy rain and dramatic storm surge leaving communities along the Panhandle in shambles.

Gov. Ron DeSantis said about 95% of customers who lost power during Hurricane Isaias had been restored.

The storm left more than 400,000 Florida customers without power at one point during landfall on Oct. 9.

Over 20,000 customers remained without power Wednesday morning, primarily in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties, according to PowerOutage.com.

In Escambia County alone, initial damage assessments following the damaging hurricane are estimating approximately $64 million in costs for county repairs, emergency response and recovery efforts.

Florida’s state-led Hurricane Isaias recovery effort is shifting from immediate response to aftermath impacts like debris removal, damage assessments and aid distribution across the Panhandle.
