skincare-scheme-mazal-group-investigatio:
By

Caley Fox Shannon

,

Monika Evstatieva

It's a familiar experience for anyone who has walked through an American shopping mall: A friendly salesperson approaches with a free sample of skincare cream, offering the promise of younger-looking skin. As you pass, they launch into a stream of chatter — a compliment on your handbag or a question about what's in your shopping bag. It's the kind of encounter that shoppers often walk away from without a second thought.

But behind this familiar mall ritual, NPR uncovered something far more costly: customers hit with thousands of dollars in charges they never authorized and products they didn't want and can't return.

In Michigan, an elderly man with dementia was charged $42,000 for skincare products and devices. His family didn't realize the situation until his credit score dropped, his son told NPR.

In New Mexico, a spa employee sold a woman a $30,000 red-light therapy device. She alleged in a lawsuit that he also charged $78,000 for what he said was sales tax without her consent.

In Hawaii, a disabled woman was shown to the back room of a spa for a "free" facial. The salesperson took her walker, she wrote in a complaint to the state, and refused to let her leave for hours until she spent $2,600.

These stories share a common thread: The stores they visited have contracts to buy skincare products from Mazal Group, a California-based company managing dozens of brands sold in thousands of stores worldwide. And those brands are all owned by one family.

Credit:  Bronson Arcuri/NPR

Over the past year, NPR spoke with more than 50 people impacted by this enterprise, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. This investigation draws from state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints that NPR obtained from agencies via Freedom of Information Act requests. NPR staff visited stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.

NPR's investigation finds that stores selling skincare products purchased from Mazal Group have routinely pressured shoppers, including older adults and people with disabilities, into buying expensive skincare products and services they did not want, could not afford or tried to refuse. The business model that a decade ago federal agents called a "credit card overcharge scheme" is active today in malls and shopping districts from Honolulu to Annapolis, Maryland.

Some store and kiosk operators have faced more serious legal consequences than consumer complaints. Federal agencies have investigated individual operators for employing young Israelis on tourist visas to sell these products, resulting in more than a dozen guilty pleas for visa fraud and money-laundering schemes. NPR reviewed social media posts and messages indicating that some stores connected to Mazal Group continue to employ salespeople on tourist visas today. The government hasn't brought similar charges for a decade, and Israel's admission to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program in 2023 has removed a key barrier to entry for unauthorized workers.

Though Mazal Group and the family behind it have publicly shifted responsibility for any wrongdoing onto individual store owners, NPR obtained documents that show their brands suggest stores sell products at abnormally high markups while adhering to a strict refund policy set by the group. And a lab test commissioned by NPR raises questions about whether some of the products they sell contain the ingredients their labels promise.

Orogold Cosmetics is a skincare brand linked to consumer complaints across the United States. The brand also operates internationally, like this Hong Kong location in Causeway Bay.
                
                    
                    SCMP Photo/SCMP via Reuters Connect/X07425
                    
                
                hide caption

Across the hundreds of complaints reviewed by NPR — filed with state attorneys general, the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Better Business Bureau and other watchdogs — customers describe their experiences in strikingly similar ways.

Their stories start with a young salesperson standing outside a store or mall kiosk offering free samples. Customers say that if they stop, the salesperson quickly escorts — and in some accounts, physically pulls — them into the store and begins a barrage of sales pitches.

In the complaints, customers describe being kept in stores for an hour or more, sometimes isolated in a back room, while salespeople refuse to take no for an answer. The products carry no price tags, they say, which frees the salesperson to negotiate "special sales" and throw in "free gifts" to sweeten the deal on an expensive cream, facial or red-light therapy device.

Shoppers reported to agencies that salespeople did not disclose the amount they charged at the register, which was often much higher than the agreed-upon price. One told authorities that the salesperson added a zero, increasing the sum tenfold from $1,300 to $13,000. In police reports, others allege a store employee told them their card declined when it had not and charged a second card as well.

In court cases, shoppers alleged the salesperson instructed them to sign on a tablet at checkout, not mentioning it was a final-sale policy that could be used against them in credit card disputes. Some said they were signed up for a "payment plan" that salespeople didn't disclose was really a high-interest loan. In some reports, customers said the salesperson instructed them to authorize charges flagged by their bank as potentially fraudulent.

At the bottom of the bag, many said, the salesperson buried a receipt that said, "All sales final. No refunds. No exchanges."

In official reports and NPR interviews, customers said they were left angry, stunned and ashamed at how much they were charged, from several hundred dollars to more than $100,000 in one case. Records show some customers recovered partial or full amounts through their credit card companies, while others remained on the hook for thousands. Police reports show numerous shoppers tried to escalate their complaint to authorities, but arrests were almost never made.

In written reports, customers compared the ordeal to being robbed, held hostage or physically assaulted. NPR spoke to five individuals who hid the experience from their families for months or years. One woman said she went into a period of deep depression: "I just felt like if this is the way people are, I don't want to live in a world like this."

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., in April. In 2024, Torrez filed a lawsuit against the store Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre, alleging violations of New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act.
                
                    
                    Jose Luis Magana/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

In New Mexico, Attorney General Raúl Torrez's office received dozens of complaints about a store called Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre that, he said, "painted a picture that this was a business that was just brazenly taking advantage of people."

One woman said a salesperson kept her in the store for hours until she agreed to spend $600 on products from the skincare brand Voupre. The salesperson said her credit card was declined, so she provided another. Later that day, she was "mortified" to see two charges totaling $44,280 in her banking app.

"I thought, 'How did they do that?' I really didn't know what had happened," said the 67-year-old woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of reprisal from the spa owner.

When the store would not refund her, she successfully disputed a charge for $27,000 with one credit card company. But she was responsible for $17,280 for a shopping experience she called "traumatic."

Torrez filed a lawsuit against the store in 2024, alleging violations of New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act.

"The scale of the price increases, the aggressive tactics, the repeated practice of misquoting prices and then elevating prices while refusing to return a product — we usually don't see a business that is this brazen and this out in the open, in terms of what they're trying to do to take advantage of consumers," said Torrez.

The spa's owner is Sahar Hori, an Israeli national who, according to court records, is also a U.S. citizen. Hori closed the spa and settled his case with New Mexico in 2025, agreeing to pay $350,000 in restitution to customers.

Mary Lee says she was pressured into buying $19,000 of products at Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre while on a writer's retreat. She tried to get a refund before returning home to Duluth, Minn., but she wasn't able to get her money back. This year, the store's owner paid restitution to its customers, including Lee.
                
                    
                    Caroline Yang for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

One of those customers is Mary Lee, an artist from Duluth, Minnesota. She said Hori's employees pressured her into spending nearly $19,000 on products while she was visiting Santa Fe for a writer's retreat. She said she tried to get her money back before returning home, but the refund she said a salesman promised her never came through.

The debt weighed on her like "a lead vest, an anchor," she told NPR. Lee is 65 and retired from full-time work. This year, through New Mexico's settlement, she was made whole.

"I feel a ton has been lifted off my shoulders," she said. "I don't feel like Atlas carrying the world anymore."

A small group of customers brought a second case against Hori, which settled in February 2026 for an undisclosed amount. While his customers were complaining to the New Mexico Department of Justice, financial records obtained in that lawsuit show the store's bank account was used to pay a lease to Mercedes-Benz and rent for a downtown Miami high-rise apartment. On his Instagram, Hori posted pictures of beach vacations in Europe and the Caribbean.

"Mr. Hori acknowledges that some customers were unhappy," his lawyers told NPR, "but he disputes any characterizations that his business intentionally deceived anyone."

The Beauty Essentials store in the Briarwood Mall in Ann Arbor, Mich., has since closed. Employees followed similar aggressive sales tactics by pressuring customers to spend thousands of dollars on products.
                
                    
                    Rosem Morton for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

The aggressive tactics documented in Santa Fe are replicated in shopping centers nationwide.

In Ann Arbor, Mich., Michele Anliker said her elderly mother was "preyed upon" at a Briarwood Mall store called Beauty Essentials during a 2024 Christmas trip, ultimately leaving with $5,000 in Voupre skincare products she did not want. When Anliker confronted the employees, she said, they accused her mother of stealing.

Michele Anliker's elderly mother was pressured into spending $5,000 on products she didn't want in 2024. Anliker then mobilized her local community and rallied over 30 local victims.
                
                    
                    Rosem Morton for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Anliker complained to mall management, filed a police report and distributed flyers warning shoppers away from Beauty Essentials. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. It wasn't until she escalated the situation to the mall's owner, Simon Property Group, that she secured a refund.

Cheryle Grounds' 84-year-old father was unable to recover the almost $10,000 he spent at Beauty Essentials on New Year's Day 2025. He has poor hearing and eyesight, and he walks the mall for exercise. Grounds told NPR that her father believed he bought a facial package but was also charged for Voupre items he understood to be gifts with purchase.

Grounds and Anliker declined to identify their parents by name, citing privacy concerns for their elderly parents.

In 2025, Cheryle Grounds' father was pressured into spending almost $10,000 on products at Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor.
                
                    
                    Rosem Morton for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

In Manhattan Beach, Calif., 82-year-old retired teacher Mary Ellen Eckhert — who uses a motorized wheelchair — stopped for a free sample outside the store Mia's by Voupre. She would return to the spa for regular facials over the next year, where store employees ultimately charged her $53,500 across four credit cards, including $24,045 on one visit.

"What kind of a spa charges anyone $54,000?" said her son, Marc Eckhert, who discovered the charges after his mother's bank account overdrew. While the family managed to dispute much of the debt, Mary Ellen Eckhert remains out more than $17,000.

"I'm feeling like I have to continue working in order to pay for all this," she said.

NPR reached out to the former owner of Beauty Essentials, Guy Gabay, and did not receive a response. The store closed in 2025. The Briarwood Mall and Simon Property Group did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

NPR visited Mia's by Voupre and reached representative Daniella Vanon by phone, who declined to comment. The Manhattan Village Mall, where the store is located, did not respond to NPR.

Mazal Group owner Daphna Weingarten and her husband, Eli Weingarten, attend the Vine Vera launch party in Century City, Calif., in 2012.
                
                    
                    Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

While Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre, Beauty Essentials and Mia's by Voupre were independently owned and located thousands of miles apart, the stores all sold customers Voupre products, a brand sold exclusively by Mazal Group in Chatsworth, California.

The company is a family business, owned by Daphna Oded Weingarten, who operates the group alongside her husband, Eli Weingarten; her brother, Avihu Oded; and his ex-wife, Adi Sharvit Oded.

Mazal translates to "luck" or "good fortune" in Hebrew. The Weingartens and Odeds are originally from Israel, as are the majority of corporate employees and licensees (store owners), according to former staff members.

Five former corporate employees agreed to speak with NPR on the condition of anonymity, fearing retaliation from Mazal Group. A small cohort of non-Israelis staffs the design, engineering and marketing departments, they said, as well as the on-site warehouse that fulfills orders.

The Weingartens and Odeds founded their first brand together in 2005 — a line of hair straighteners called HerStyler, under the company HerStyler Inc. A host of sister brands soon followed, and various other companies to house those brands. In 2015, Daphna Weingarten established Mazal Group to centralize operations for the family's growing portfolio.

The family currently holds more than 50 active trademarks for skin and hair care brands. Among the most prominent are Voupre, Avinichi, Introstem, CbGäRDN, Venofye, Lionesse and Orogold Cosmetics, which sell a nearly identical line of products.

Loading...

"The reason why they have so many brands is because they had to keep remaking brands with different names to sell it a different way to the malls so that they could get a lease," one former employee told NPR.

Another said store owners who purchased from Mazal Group distanced themselves from a brand once it started to accumulate bad reviews and complaints.

"People would complain about a line, about a brand being destroyed and having a bad reputation," the former worker said. "So they would constantly come out with something fresh, something new."

Adi Sharvit Oded and Avihu Oded pose for a picture at an Orogold Cosmetics event in 2014. The couple is now divorced, but public records show they continue to hold business licenses alongside Avihu Oded's family members, Daphna Oded Weingarten and Eli Weingarten.
                
                    
                    Facebook/Screenshot by NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

A former corporate employee said it's difficult to measure Mazal Group's precise global footprint because stores open and close frequently, but estimated the company contracts with at least 2,000 stores worldwide.

While reporting this story, NPR attempted to reach the Weingartens, Odeds and Mazal Group via phone and email, as well as visiting the Chatsworth headquarters to request an interview. They did not acknowledge this outreach until NPR sent a letter describing its findings, and lawyers for the group provided a brief statement.

"Mazal Group does not own or operate any retail locations that sell cosmetic products or any other products for that matter. Nor does Mazal Group manufacture any products," said Brian Tilker of the firm Cox Fricke in Hawaii.

Mazal Group looms large in the skincare kiosk industry, but it's not the only player in the market. Premier Dead Sea, an Israel-based skincare company, was once widespread in U.S. malls but has scaled back its footprint in recent years. Its subsidiary, Avologi, manufactures many of the red-light therapy devices that customers reported being pressured to buy inside stores contracted with Mazal Group.

Premier Dead Sea and Avologi also did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.

Federal agencies have investigated crimes associated with the Israeli-owned skincare industry in the past, but a lack of sustained and coordinated oversight has allowed it to thrive from coast to coast.

In 2010, the U.S. Embassy in Tel Aviv, Israel, sent a cable to the Department of Homeland Security warning of fraudulent activity linked to the "Dead Sea industry," which had spread to 36 states.

The term refers to the many Israeli-owned stores and kiosks that were marketing the benefits of products made with salt or minerals from the Dead Sea. The Odeds and Weingartens faced competition from companies like Premier Dead Sea, which was also gaining a foothold in the States with its own family of brands.

A kiosk that Shai Cohen leased at a mall in Virginia.
                
                    
                    U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia
                    
                
                hide caption

In the cable, published by WikiLeaks, the embassy said recruiters in Israel were targeting young people finishing mandatory military service and promising large sums to be made working at American malls. The workers were coached to lie to U.S. consular and border officials to obtain a tourist visa and travel to the U.S. without work authorization, the cable reads. In the States, they were paid under the table and store owners failed to withhold or pay required payroll taxes on their wages, it continues.

The embassy also released a series of public service announcements on YouTube in 2011, featuring the cautionary tales of young Israelis who had been caught by U.S. authorities for illegally working on tourist visas and were either deported or later denied reentry to the United States.

Soon after, federal agencies coordinated to investigate two businesses selling products from brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds for immigration and financial crimes. The combined efforts of the departments of Labor, State and Homeland Security, the FBI and the IRS culminated in raids, international extraditions and more than a dozen guilty pleas.

In a 2013 operation code-named "Salty Winds," a task force of federal agents surveilled stores and apartments leased to Israeli national Shai Cohen in the D.C.-Maryland-Virginia region. Cohen had kiosks selling Vine Vera and Orogold Cosmetics, brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds, as well as locations selling Premier Dead Sea and its affiliates.

Cohen's enterprise employed an estimated 60 unauthorized workers and brought in nearly $4 million between 2011 and 2013, according to federal records.

Cohen, two managers and at least seven salespeople engaged in fraudulent marriages to stay in the country long term, according to a Department of Labor interview of Cohen's business partner that NPR obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request. One salesman paid an American woman working at another store in the mall $10,000 to marry him.

Special Agent Matt Grimm stands outside the U.S. District Court in Alexandria, Virginia. He was an investigator for the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General and led the task force investigating Shai Cohen's business practices.
                
                    
                    Michael Noble Jr. for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Special Agent Matt Grimm, then an investigator for the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General, led the task force. Grimm recently retired from the Army's Criminal Investigation Division.

While agents were pursuing immigration fraud and tax evasion charges, they also documented a "credit card overcharge scheme" used to dupe shoppers at Cohen's stores.

"There's no price tag," said Grimm, who observed sales and made purchases himself. "Whatever the salesperson on the spot thinks that they can charge for a particular thing, they're going to get. The more they sell, the higher their commission is going to be."

In a Christmastime raid, Grimm's team arrested a dozen young Israelis working at Cohen's stores on tourist visas. The store owner was in Israel at the time, triggering a yearslong extradition process.

Shai Cohen, an Israeli national, leased several stores and kiosks in the Washington, D.C., area. He employed an estimated 60 unauthorized workers and brought in nearly $4 million between 2011 and 2013, according to federal records.
                
                    
                    U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia
                    
                
                hide caption

Cohen pleaded guilty in 2023 in Virginia to conspiracy to launder money and facilitate the illegal entry, harboring and transporting of noncitizens. He served 11 months of a two-year prison sentence. NPR tried to reach Cohen through his real estate business in Israel and did not receive a response.

One of Cohen's contemporaries was another Israeli national, named Omer Gur, owner of a larger group of stores along the East Coast, including Orogold Cosmetics locations.

"Instead of looking at one kiosk or one store in one location, we wanted to cut the head off the snake," FBI Special Agent Sara Shalowitz said of Gur.

Shalowitz led a team that covertly surveilled Gur's stores for three years before apprehending him in Raleigh, N.C., as he attempted to board a one-way international flight.

Gur pleaded guilty in 2016 to a visa fraud and money-laundering conspiracy that included over 140 unauthorized workers and earned more than $14 million, according to the Justice Department. He was sentenced to 6.5 years in prison and served 30 months. A dozen of his associates pleaded guilty on related charges, Shalowitz said.

"I think we set a real deterrence for why this matters," Shalowitz told NPR. "It's not just some administrative thing to come to the U.S. under false pretenses, defraud numerous agencies … for the profit of your business and your business partners, at the expense of violating U.S. law."

NPR reached Gur, who also works in real estate in Israel, by phone. He declined to comment.

Cohen's and Gur's prison sentences may not have been a lasting deterrent for store owners or prospective salespeople.

On Facebook groups and Instagram pages, recruiters advertise jobs working in mall kiosks, or "agalot" — Hebrew for "carts." They promise young people the opportunity to bring in a high income and live in American cities with others their age. One account posts memes about the highs and lows of working in the agalot: long hours, difficult customers and boatloads of money to be made.

A meme that highlights the good life in the skincare industry.
                
                    
                    Agalot Life/Screenshot by NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

A young Israeli man posted a video to YouTube in November 2025 describing his last three months working at a store that sells Introstem, a brand owned by the Weingartens and Odeds and distributed by Mazal Group. NPR confirmed the store location in a Texas mall through photographs on his social media accounts.

"There is a lot of money in the agalot," he said. "A seller who is good after a few months, you sharpen your skills, and you become an expert. You can make $10,000 a month like it's nothing."

He described having a company vehicle and furnished apartment, with rent deducted from his pay. Workers make a 30% commission on their sales, he said.

"It's hard work, not easy," he said. "But it's a good job considering the fact that you can print money just based on your silver tongue."

NPR reached the 20-year-old to request an interview. He said he wanted payment, which NPR does not do. NPR is not using his name because it would expose him to federal officials for immigration crimes that he admits to in the video.

"It's illegal," he said. "Why is it illegal? Because you are tourists. You are on a tourist visa, and you come to work."

"But immigration authorities aren't looking for us. Immigration is looking for the Mexicans who sell drugs, less for the Israelis who contribute to their economy."

NPR staff also engaged online with recruiters for stores selling the Weingartens and Odeds' products. One, hiring for a store selling their brand Lionesse in South Carolina, told NPR staff to obtain a visa before they could share more details about the job. They "don't help with visas," the recruiter said.

Between the lines is the suggestion to work on a tourist visa, legal experts told NPR. Companies legally employing foreign staff submit mandatory paperwork to the State Department for nonimmigrant work visas.

Travel to the U.S. has also become easier for Israelis since Israel's 2023 admission to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program. Most Israelis can now visit the U.S. for up to 90 days for business or tourism, visa-free, by completing a short online application 72 hours before travel.

"That removes a key step in the recruitment process," said Grimm, who previously served as a diplomatic security special agent with the Department of State. Since most Israelis no longer need to interview with a U.S. consular official before departure, he said, "it's as simple as getting on the airplane and going. But, you're still not authorized to work."

NPR reached out to the departments of Homeland Security, Labor and State, the IRS and the FBI to comment on whether they continue to investigate Israeli-owned skincare stores for federal crimes. They would not say whether oversight or enforcement is ongoing.

NPR contacted dozens of current and former salespeople at stores selling products from Mazal Group to hear their side of the story. None agreed to be interviewed, even on the condition of anonymity. Two asked to be paid, which NPR declined.

NPR also reached out to Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs to ask whether it is taking action to discourage unauthorized work in the U.S. or address recruitment pipelines.

"The State of Israel unequivocally opposes violations of U.S. law, including U.S. immigration law," said Ester Buzgan, deputy spokesperson for the ministry. "Israeli citizens seeking employment in the United States must hold a valid work visa and comply fully with the law."

Suzann Roberts holds a paper bag of Voupre skincare products from Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Michigan.
                
                    
                    Rosem Morton for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Because the stores it sells products to are independently owned and operated, Mazal Group claims it isn't responsible for the customer experience. But the company recently settled a class action lawsuit that made public reams of evidence showing that Mazal Group is directly involved in store operations and sets top-down policies that impact shoppers.

Attorneys for a class of former customers filed suit in 2022 in the 1st Circuit Court of Hawaii, alleging Mazal Group, the Weingartens and Odeds, and store owners in the state violated consumer protection laws via a "predatory and systematically unfair and deceptive enterprise."

Mazal Group asked the judge, unsuccessfully, to dismiss the case on the grounds that the company is merely a distributor that "drop ships" products for a "third-party" and owns no brands of its own.

The Weingarten and Oded family directly owns brands and manages the operations of those brands through Mazal Group. And the company's website advertises services beyond distribution, including product development, marketing, leasing, customer relations and accounting.

NPR confirmed with former Mazal Group employees that the company helps store owners secure retail space in malls and assists with the design and layout of individual locations. The company's marketing team designs product packaging and manages brand websites and social media accounts, they said.

Skincare products on display at the Orogold store opening at the Copley Place mall in Boston in 2013. The store has since closed.
                
                    
                    Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

"The Mazal Group owners and officers are involved in every step of the process, from product design to distribution to store design and development to sales to post-sale concerns," concluded a research firm hired by the plaintiffs' attorneys.

Mazal Group's agreements with stores also reveal a direct link between company policy and customer complaints. The company requires branded stores — e.g., locations with Voupre or Lionesse in the store name — to exclusively sell products purchased from Mazal Group, adopt a refund policy determined by the group and direct all customer service inquiries to its headquarters, court records show. These agreements also establish guidelines for how salespeople should offer samples to passersby.

After four years of pretrial action, the Hawaii class action case was scheduled for a jury trial in July 2026 in Honolulu. In June, the parties announced they had reached a settlement.

Mazal Group, the Weingartens and Odeds, and two licensees in Hawaii agreed to pay $950,000 in restitution, according to a copy of the settlement agreement obtained by NPR. Mazal Group and the family are responsible for $650,000 of the total payout. After legal fees, funds will be distributed proportionately to 110 class members who filed a complaint with the state of Hawaii.

Mazal Group and the Weingartens and Odeds have denied wrongdoing, and the settlement releases them from future liability for the allegations in the case.

NPR purchased a box of Voupre Anti-Aging Rescue Solution, which retails for $1,300, to have it chemically tested.
                
                    
                    Zayrha Rodriguez/NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

To understand why salespeople can negotiate the price of a product on the fly, NPR looked into what these items actually cost to make and what's inside them.

NPR obtained internal order forms for Voupre and Avinichi — brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds and distributed via Mazal Group. These documents show the brands set manufacturer-suggested retail prices at up to 130 times the wholesale price they charge to stores. Voupre's Cannabis Caviar Transforming Mask, for example, costs $23 wholesale, with a suggested retail price of $3,000.

"Pricing at that level typically raises red flags," said Joe Rowett, CEO of VELOX, an Idaho-based marketing agency for skincare and beauty brands.

Well-known luxury brands rarely stretch the suggested retail price to even 20 times the wholesale cost, and most skincare brands operate far below that, Rowett said, making Voupre's suggested markups "highly unusual."

Federal investigators and former employees suggested to NPR that this wide margin gives salespeople the flexibility to negotiate the best sales price to earn maximum commission.

Suzann Roberts bought Voupre Anti-Aging Rescue Solution from Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Mich., in 2024, and she was unable to return the unopened box. NPR sent the product to be tested at Founders Science Group in Taunton, Massachusetts.
                
                    
                    Rosem Morton for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

NPR sent a single unopened box of a Voupre "best-seller" for chemical testing. The sample — one box of one product — is limited, but the results of the analysis raise questions about what the label promises and what the product contains.

Formulation chemist Jocelyn Chace pipettes samples for high-performance liquid chromatography machines, which were used to test a Voupre product obtained by NPR, at Founders Science Group's laboratory in Taunton, Massachusetts.
                
                    
                    Sophie Park for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Many shoppers described being lured into a store with a sample of Voupre Anti-Aging Rescue Solution, which Mazal sells to stores for $19.50 per unit with a suggested retail price of $1,300. NPR obtained an unopened box of the solution from Suzann Roberts, a 90-year-old woman in Ann Arbor who bought the product from Beauty Essentials in 2024 and was unable to return it.

NPR sent the sample to Founders Science Group in Taunton, Massachusetts. CEO Robert Munroe has worked as a pharmaceutical scientist for three decades.

By looking at the product's ingredients list, Munroe identified three ingredients for analysis that could support Voupre's anti-aging claims: vitamin A to accelerate skin-cell turnover, vitamin E to fight collagen breakdown and acetyl hexapeptide-8, a powerful peptide that some call "Botox in a bottle."

The lab could not detect any trace of vitamin A or E, which Munroe said was "surprising and definitely suspicious." Vitamin A can degrade in strength over time without proper preservatives, he said, but it's not possible for vitamin E to disappear entirely. If the manufacturer did not include the actives at production and Voupre listed them on the packaging, he said, "that would be misbranding."

Robert Munroe is the CEO of Founders Science Group, which specializes in testing cosmetic and personal care products.
                
                    
                    Sophie Park for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Based on what the lab detected, which included a high concentration of the peptide, Munroe said the solution is comparable to The Ordinary's 10% Argireline Solution, which retails for under $10.

"As far as getting peptide on the skin, you don't need to spend $1,300 to do it," he said.

The formula for Voupre's Anti-Aging Rescue Solution is the basis for nearly identical wrinkle creams that the Weingartens and Odeds sell across other brands like Introstem, CbGäRDN, Venofye and Lavelier.

Products from five different brands owned by the Weingarten and Oded family are virtually indistinguishable, and all cost around $1,300.
                
                    
                    Collage by NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

New stores selling the Weingartens and Odeds' brands crop up regularly across the U.S. and globally, especially in port cities and tourist destinations.

Complaints haven't slowed them down, one former Mazal Group employee told NPR.

"It wasn't like it was stopping the business. They were still expanding, opening, expanding, opening, expanding, opening."

The Weingartens and Odeds have also closed companies and shuttered numerous brands over the years. Just last month, Mazal Group itself — the hub of operations for the family business — terminated its business license in California.

NPR reporters visited the Chatsworth headquarters weeks before that, in August 2026. The building, which once sported a Mazal Group logo more than 10 feet high and wide, bore a similar sign saying INV Brands.

Innovation Brands Inc. was founded by Daphna and Eli Weingarten in 2024.

"Streamlining the journey from concept to consumer," the company's website reads. "We leverage global expertise to build, manage, and scale exceptional personal care brands."

Chuck Lorre, a famous producer known for series like "Two and a Half Men" and "Big Bang Theory" spoke with Joe Rogan about the importance of religious faith.

Hollywood producer Chuck Lorre, the creative force behind hit sitcoms such as "Two and a Half Men" and "The Big Bang Theory," discussed the importance of spirituality on Joe Rogan's podcast Tuesday.

Lorre released his memoir, "Sitcom: A Memoir," on Tuesday, reflecting on his life and career. Lorre has previously discussed his religious background, having been raised Jewish before joining the Church of Scientology in his youth and later embracing Buddhism.

In the most recent episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience," Lorre warned that worldly wealth and fame ultimately are not fulfilling and that "it's not the real solution. The real solution, you know, I'm going to say it and then regret it, but the real solution is a spiritual solution. You have to find something beyond this world."

After Rogan asked why he might regret making the remark, including whether it had to do with working in Hollywood, Lorre replied that he didn't wish to be associated with "new age bulls---."

RICHARD GERE CONFRONTS HOLLYWOOD FAME, EGO AND GREED AS 'DARK CLOUDS' THAT THREATEN INNER PEACE

Chuck Lorre spills secrets from his life and from his many sets in his new memoir, "Sitcom." (Presley Ann/Getty Images for Lucas Museum of Narrative Art)

Rogan agreed, saying he believes the term "spirituality" has been co-opted by insincere people who have given it a "bad name."

"I know some people that are like legitimately spiritual. Some of the nicest people that I know," Rogan said, describing a Christian acquaintance who built homes for homeless people and helped them overcome addiction.

"It's like I know people like that too," Lorre agreed. "They're real, and they’re role models."

Later on in the episode, Lorre marveled at how humans are unlike animals in that they create religions as a means of understanding and valuing the world around them, saying, "You wanna call it true or not, it's an organizing element that no other animal does."

'WIZARDS OF WAVERLY PLACE' STAR DAVID HENRIE SAYS HIS FAITH COST HIM AGENTS, MONEY AND FRIENDS IN HOLLYWOOD

Television producer Chuck Lorre accepts an award onstage during Project Angel Food’s Angel Awards at The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation Campus on Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Project Angel Food)

"When civilizations or cultures that took God out of the picture, they replaced it, with the Communist Party, with a fascist dictator. You know, it's the same idea: ‘Organize around me. Doesn’t matter if I’m right or not, organize around me.’ And people will," he warned.

Lorre compared shared religious beliefs to a tent pole holding society's understanding of reality together, suggesting that challenging those beliefs can provoke anger and uncertainty.

"And if you take that away from them, they get angry. It freaks them out because it's like the tent pole. As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense and energy emerging as key growth markets.

The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation.

The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process.

In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview.

Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch.

“Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.”

Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries.

About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said.

The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Simplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago.

Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said.

Energy, electronics and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry.

Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China.

The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project.

With its latest funding, Scimplify plans to deploy around $7.5 million for its U.S. expansion, including building out its manufacturing network, Santhosh said. It also earmarked another $2 million for further development of Scinode.

The startup employs about 340 people, including roughly 70 scientists. Most of its workforce is based in India, though it also has local teams in the U.S., Japan, Indonesia, and the UAE.

Midfielder Leticia McKenna bagged a first-half brace to bolster her case for a first 2027 Women's World Cup call-up as the Matildas overcame Haiti 7–1.

Fresh off a humbling 4–2 defeat to powerhouses Germany, and without Arsenal star Steph Catley (managed), Australia got their World Cup preparations back on track in Chambly, France.

A plane passenger has sparked a fierce debate about window seat etiquette after clashing with a crying child onboard.

Sharna Kite recently took to TikTok to share her vexing encounter with a fellow traveler.

But just seconds later, the hand of a toddler in the row in front reaches behind him to pull it back down.

The tot can be heard crying and whimpering in the background as Kite once again raises the shade.

The young boy continues to grumble as he and Kite become locked in battle as each repeatedly reaches for it in turn.

Eventually, Kite appears to hold the blind up in place and, with the boy unable to out-muscle her, he lets out a disgruntled squeal.

Kite added overlaid text that read: 'Unfortunately no, I will not be the bigger person.'

A plane passenger has sparked a fierce debate about window seat etiquette after clashing with a crying child onboard (stock image)

The video, which has so far been viewed more than 7.4 million times, sparked a firestorm in the comments.

On the one hand, there were some who thought Kite was in the wrong for not allowing the kid to get his own way.

'Everyone saying kids are so annoying but have we thought about how the kid might be annoyed too?' one wrote.

'I just realized nearly everyone doesn't treat kids as beings, this is disgusting,' another added.

'No because if you don't want the light buy a sleep mask or drape something over your eyes. If I have a window seat I want to look out of my window,' a third said.

Capitol Hill was given a MAGA makeover after President Donald Trump took office.

But now there is a new trend sweeping through the world of plastic surgery that stands in direct contention.

The 'anti-Mar-a-Lago' face.

Dr Melinda Lacerna Kimbrell, a double board-certified plastic surgeon and owner of LA Plastic Surgery, has spoken to the Daily Mail about the new trend.

Capitol Hill was given a MAGA makeover after President Donald Trump took office. Pictured: Kristi Noem in 2025

The specialist, who has performed more than 1,000 facelifts, defined the look as being 'relaxed rather than armored.'

'The brows sit naturally and still move, the eyes look open rather than pulled, the cheeks have shape without looking inflated, and the lips remain proportionate to the rest of the face.

'The jawline may be defined, but it should not look carved or unnaturally tight,' she shared.

But the most important feature of the 'anti-Mar-a-Lago' face is that the person remains recognizable.

'You should notice that he or she looks rested, healthy and refreshed — not immediately begin counting the procedures,' Dr Kimbrell explained.

'The anti-Mar-a-Lago face isn't anti-plastic surgery. It is anti-obvious plastic surgery. It is the difference between wearing the work and benefiting from it.'

She suggested that Emma Stone, Anne Hathaway and Lindsay Lohan 'all embody the refreshed-but-recognizable look from a purely aesthetic standpoint... without suggesting that any particular person has undergone a procedure.'

(Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Biden-era green bank grants worth $20 billion remain frozen two months after an appeals court ruled against the Trump administration’s attempt to cancel them.

The full U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit voted 6–4 on Aug. 4 to uphold an order blocking the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) from terminating the Inflation Reduction Act grants, finding the agency “likely contravened the IRA’s mandatory appropriation.” Days later, the court agreed to the administration’s request to keep the money frozen while it prepares to take the fight to the Supreme Court.

“The Supreme Court should absolutely take this case,” Jason Isaac, CEO of the American Energy Institute, said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation. “The Biden administration rushed $20 billion in taxpayer money into the hands of politically connected organizations, creating what looks like a taxpayer-funded slush fund for its climate agenda.”

“At a time when so many Americans are struggling to afford skyrocketing utility bills, the Trump administration is refusing to implement this program, which would lower bills for those who most need the help,” Mark Drajem, media director at the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), said in a statement to the DCNF. “That’s a cruel blow from this administration made worse by the fact that the president had pledged to cut energy bills.”

The stay pauses the part of the court’s order that would require the money to be paid out through Nov. 9, according to Columbia Law School’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. It will be extended until the Supreme Court acts if the administration files a petition, and the grantees did not oppose it. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Biden’s ‘Gold Bars’ Went To Politically-Connected Orgs Over Internal Red Flags, Watchdog Finds)

The EPA, Climate United and the offices of Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey did not immediately respond to the DCNF’s requests for comment.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin canceled the grants in March 2025, citing “well documented concerns about self-dealing and conflicts of interest,” according to the agency. Climate United, the largest recipient, had been awarded about $7 billion.

A three-judge panel of the same court sided with the EPA in September 2025, ruling 2-1 that the grantees’ main claims were “essentially contractual” and belonged in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims.

The four judges in the minority in August would have lifted that part of the order, pointing to Congress’s repeal of the section that created the program in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Reuters reported. After the ruling, the EPA said it was reviewing its next steps.

“It was painful to see EPA staffers talk about getting grants out the door like they were throwing gold bars off the Titanic, but that’s the predictable result when the government spends your money,” Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the Cato Institute, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“Resource-neutral permitting reform is superior to subsidies and grants because it advances energy projects without the government picking winners and losers (and creating far too much wasteful spending),” Fisher said. “With permitting reform, it’s also much easier for builders to trust that the rules won’t change every four years.”

“The claim that government-funded green banks lower energy costs is laughable,” Isaac said. “Taking money from taxpayers, funneling it through politically connected middlemen, and subsidizing technologies that struggle to compete in the marketplace doesn’t make energy more affordable.”

The NRDC which supports the program, argues the opposite.

“The economic costs of this go far beyond the $20 billion, because these funds would unlock billions of dollars more in private investments,” Drajem said.

The program could bring in $65.5 billion in total investment and save consumers $52 billion on energy costs over 20 years, according to a May 2025 analysis by Energy Innovation, an energy and climate policy think tank.

“Affordability comes from abundant, reliable energy and competition, not government handouts to politically favored organizations,” Isaac said in his statement to the DCNF. “The Supreme Court has an opportunity to address serious questions about executive oversight of these grants and protect taxpayers from being treated like an unlimited ATM for the Democrats’ agenda.”

“Instead of continuing this senseless attack on this program, the administration should end its attack on affordable energy and get these funds out to the homeowners and renters who desperately need them,” Drajem said. “If it keeps fighting in court that will demonstrate, yet again, that it doesn’t care about lowering people’s energy costs.”

Green banks have kept lending without the federal money. They financed $12.4 billion in projects in 2024 and 2025, about $11 billion of it from private investors, according to the U.S. Green Bank 50, a coalition of 56 green banks and other organizations, Canary Media reported. (RELATED: Appeals Court Dunks On Tanya Chutkan For Thwarting Trump Admin Attempt To Claw Back Biden’s ‘Gold Bars’)

“We’re making a virtue out of a necessity,” Dan Adler, the group’s executive director, told the outlet.

Climate United has been unable to follow through on plans to finance U.S.-built electric trucks, energy-efficiency and clean energy upgrades, and loans to Native American-led clean energy projects, according to Canary Media.

Climate United said after the August ruling that despite “false allegations and misinformation, there remains no legal basis for terminating our grant award,” according to Reuters.

Democrats cheered the August ruling. Sens. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island as well as Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan said in an Aug. 4 joint statement that it stopped the Trump administration’s “brazen attempt to prevent those projects, seize these funds, and break the law in the process.”

Two federal district courts in September also vacated the EPA’s termination of Solar for All, a separate $7 billion program funded through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, according to the Sabin Center.

lionesses-texas-prisons-ac:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two years after his release from prison, Patrick Dewayne Smith spends Sundays with his family in a modest brick church with a white steeple in rural Tennessee. He works two jobs. He goes to ball games to cheer for nieces and nephews he had never met. After serving 13 years for a nonviolent drug conviction, he is trying to rebuild his life.

Now Smith could be sent back to prison for the rest of it.

A federal judge released him in 2024 under rules adopted after Congress passed the First Step Act, a landmark criminal justice law during President Donald Trump’s first term. But the Supreme Court ruled in May that people sentenced under older, harsher laws cannot rely on the disparity between their sentences and current penalties to seek early compassionate release.

“Every time I get a call, I’m hoping it’s some good news. Or, you know, at least not no bad news,” said Smith, a tall, soft-spoken 47-year-old whose beard is now flecked with gray.

Smith is among about a dozen people nationwide who could be returned to prison because of the ruling, according to FAMM, a sentencing reform group formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums. Without clemency from the White House, the group says, second chances could disappear for those people.

The First Step Act was the most significant rewrite of federal sentencing laws in a generation. Among other changes, it reduced some lengthy mandatory minimum sentences, particularly for nonviolent drug crimes. Trump said the law would “make our communities safer and give former inmates a second chance at life after they have served their time.”

The law was championed by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser who had a personal connection to the issue: Kushner’s his father had spent time in federal prison when Kushner was younger.

Thousands of people have been released from prison in the years since the law was passed, but some recent Supreme Court rulings have made it harder for other people already serving long sentences to argue for their release. For Smith and others like him, competing interpretations have created a high-stakes legal limbo.

“They’re doing everything that they should be doing. They’re reestablishing relationships with families. They’re volunteering in their communities. They’re working,” said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM’s general counsel. “Having them reincarcerated is so unjust given that they have demonstrated their rehabilitation.”

Without a grant of clemency from the White House, Rifkin says their second chance could be snatched away.

Trump remains proud of signing the First Step Act, and the administration is actively reviewing developments, said a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.

In 2023, the U.S. Sentencing Commission adopted new rules for people serving unusually long sentences. Judges could sometimes consider changes to the law when deciding whether to grant compassionate release to inmates who had served at least 10 years.

Not everyone agreed.

The Department of Justice argued the new rules went beyond what the First Step Act allowed. Judges nevertheless agreed to free dozens of people across the country after considering legal changes and other factors, FAMM found.

The dispute eventually went all the way to the Supreme Court, which handed down a 6-3 decision in May. It found that sentencing disparities from decades past are not “extraordinary and compelling” reasons to grant compassionate release.

“It is hard to see how Congress’s deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that ‘warrant(s)’ a reduction,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for the conservative majority.

The decision was one of two during the last Supreme Court term that narrowed the options for people serving long sentences, said Daniel Harawa, a law professor at New York University. “I worry a lot about what this means for federal criminal justice reform,” he said.

For Smith and about a dozen other people around the country, it could mean they have to finish serving a sentence that would not be handed down today.

Smith grew up in a small town in rural northern Alabama and became addicted to drugs as a teenager, his lawyers said in court documents. At 17, he was arrested for selling crack cocaine twice to an informant. A pair of marijuana convictions followed a few years later. He served about three years in prison. After his release, he worked as a construction worker and a janitor.

In 2010, he got involved with a drug ring selling crack cocaine and marijuana on the Tennessee-Alabama line, prosecutors said. Caught on phone calls recorded by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, he was convicted of drug conspiracy and money laundering after he pulled out of a plea deal that called for 12 years to 14 years in prison in exchange for his cooperation.

His lawyers called his involvement “unremarkable,” but the federal conviction combined with his prior record triggered a life sentence.

The judge questioned whether the punishment fit the crime, but said the laws tied her hands. It was the longest sentence linked to the 20-person case, exceeding even the ringleader’s.

Smith said he resolved to keep his head down behind bars, working prison jobs and avoiding infractions.

“What kept me sane was that faith, that belief in God,” he said.

He missed little things, like sleeping in a full-sized bed and taking a bath after a long day. He missed big things, too: His mother died during his first year in prison and he couldn’t ask his family to shoulder the $1,000 it would cost for him to travel home for the funeral.

After the Sentencing Commission adopted its new compassionate release rules following the First Step Act, Smith asked a judge for a reduction to time served. It took nearly a year, but the court agreed he should go free.

He returned to Alabama and moved in with his sister and her daughter.

Last month, prosecutors filed court documents challenging his release and they pointed to the Supreme Court decision. They argued he would be subject to a mandatory-minimum sentence of 25 years, even under current laws, and called the judge’s decision to release him “difficult to justify.”

A Justice Department official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing case said Rutherford’s case means his release is no longer valid, and the department cannot agree to a sentence below what the law requires.

The prospect of a return to prison is a bitter pill for his father, James Smith, a mainstay at the Willow Grove Missionary Baptist Church.

“When you got rapists and murderers and you get this guy on a nonviolent case and you want him for life,” he said, “it doesn’t sit well with me.”

Green Party of Vancouver mayoral hopeful Pete Fry is supposed to be the progressive voter’s candidate of choice this election. After several meetings this summer, two other progressive parties — OneCity and the Coalition of Progressive Electors, or COPE — pulled their mayoral candidates to try to avoid splitting the vote and handing incumbent Mayor Ken Sim another victory.

One lucky Tyee reader will get to choose from six great reads for kids and teens.

So why are some prominent former progressive politicians endorsing one of Fry’s opponents?

Last week a public letter endorsing Rebecca Bligh for mayor was signed by Mike Harcourt, former Vancouver mayor and former BC NDP premier; Peter Ladner, former Non-Partisan Association city councillor and Vancouver mayoral candidate; and Geoff Meggs, former Vision Vancouver city councillor and later chief of staff for previous BC NDP premier John Horgan.

Brenda Bailey, a former BC NDP MLA who decided not to run for re-election in the provincial campaign, has also endorsed Bligh, according to a post on Bailey’s Facebook account.

“Vancouver deserves a mayor who listens and hears them, and can work through disagreements and get the job done,” the letter reads. “Rebecca Bligh is that leader.”

The latest two polls for the mayoral race show the race is largely between Sim and Fry. A Leger poll commissioned by the Vancouver Sun shows Pete Fry at 23 per cent support compared with Ken Sim at 19 per cent, with other mayoral candidates Bligh, Kareem Allam and Colleen Hardwick all around 5 to 6 per cent support.

A Canada Pulse Insights poll commissioned by CityNews and Omni puts Fry at 28 per cent support and Sim at 27 per cent. That poll shows 19 per cent support for Allam, 13 per cent support for Hardwick and seven per cent support for Bligh.

The former politicians cited Bligh’s eight years of experience on city council, as well as her two-year stint as president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, which ended this past June.

But in both the letter and in interviews with The Tyee, Harcourt, Meggs and Ladner acknowledged Bligh’s gender was also a factor in their decision.

“It’s about time to have a woman mayor in Vancouver after a hundred and some odd years,” said Harcourt.

“And she just happens to be the most qualified to be mayor anyways, with her two terms on council and an excellent, well-regarded stint as the head of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. I think she’d be a far better mayor than Ken Sim.”

The letter also endorsed a slate of council candidates, including Vote Vancouver’s Rebecca Hasdell, John Boychuk, Steve Jedreicich and Geoff Teoli; OneCity Vancouver’s Iona Bonamis, Frances Bula, Jarrett Hagglund and Lucy Maloney; and the Vancouver Liberals’ Moira Stilwell.

“My interest in this was to shine what I think is a deserving light on people who I think could work well with Rebecca Bligh,” Geoff Meggs said, adding he personally supports OneCity’s Caitlin Stockwell for council but had to reach a compromise with Ladner and Harcourt for the limited council seats.

The letter was organized and distributed via email to news media by David Helliwell, a local tech entrepreneur, who told The Tyee it was part of his year-and-a-half effort to work across partisan politics to “make things work better” in the city.

“I’ve voted for pretty much everybody over the years. I don’t like partisan politics, but I care deeply about the city and government,” Helliwell said.

Asked for comment on the endorsement, Fry told The Tyee via text message that he was focusing on his own campaign and that he did not have relationships with Meggs, Ladner and Harcourt as Bligh did.

Fry has received an endorsement from the Vancouver and District Labour Council, a coveted election-season endorsement for progressive candidates. The VDLC represents 90 unions and their members, including workers employed by the City of Vancouver.

Endorsing a multi-partisan council slate

Both Ladner, who served on council from 2005 until he ran for mayor in 2008, and Bligh had been members of the centre-right, now-defunct Non-Partisan Association municipal party.

Ladner left municipal politics after he lost the mayoral election to Vision Vancouver’s Gregor Robertson. Bligh left the Non-Partisan Association in 2019, a year after she was first elected to council, because of what she saw as the party’s “far-right” turn.

Bligh joined ABC Vancouver for the 2022 election, after Sim also left the Non-Partisan Association to start the new party. But she was kicked out of ABC in 2025 after she voted against a motion to pause hearing new supportive-housing development pitches at council.

“I think she’d be the best mayor of all the people running,” said Ladner, who added he has voted for many different municipal parties since his time on council.

In an interview with The Tyee, Bligh said she met Harcourt early in her time on council when then-mayor Kennedy Stewart invited Harcourt to speak to council about cross-partisan and collaborative governance. They have stayed in touch ever since.

“And Geoff Meggs was somebody that I’ve asked about the viaducts, for example, and the future of the northeast False Creek development,” she said.

The letter acknowledges that outside of their endorsement of Bligh and the council candidates, Ladner, Meggs and Harcourt often disagree on politics. While they did not serve on council together, Meggs and Ladner were members of opposing parties.

But before coming out in support of Bligh, Ladner, Harcourt and Meggs told The Tyee they were supporting OneCity mayoral candidate William Azaroff.

Three progressive municipal parties running a mayoral candidate, OneCity, the Greens and COPE, had previously agreed to run just one mayoral candidate between them in an effort not to split the vote.

A little over a month ago Azaroff and COPE mayoral candidate Stephanie Allen dropped out of the race, leaving Fry as the sole progressive candidate.

“I really would have supported William Azaroff had he not dropped out in what I think was a mistake by OneCity and others that thought that Pete Fry would be able to carry this campaign,” Meggs said, adding the progressive parties should not have coalesced behind one candidate.

“If he is able to, I’d be surprised.”

When it comes to policies, Fry has criticized Bligh for her past support of closing the city’s renter office in 2023. Bligh has responded that at the time, she thought the plan to fund an external renter support organization would provide better service for renters, but she now supports reopening the city’s office because of the redevelopment pressures created by the Broadway Plan.

There are other notable differences in the parties’ platforms.

Vote Vancouver's platform doesn't mention anything about the police budget, accountability or oversight and is in favour of the school liaison officer program. On the campaign trail, Bligh has said that Vancouver pays more for police per resident than other cities and that there has been “complete mismanagement” in what police are prioritizing.

On policing, the Greens have promised to regularly report back to council from the police board on budgets, strategic priorities, community safety outcomes and performance; introduce regular independent public performance reviews of the Vancouver Police Department budget; and review the school liaison officer program or any police partnership with schools using evidence, student safety, community input and the school board's education mandate.

The Greens have also promised to implement a peer-based intervention program for people experiencing mental health or addictions issues instead of calling the police or an ambulance, and an office of community safety to integrate police, fire, licensing, property use and planning departments.

Vote Vancouver is promising a community safety strategy and more co-ordination between police and existing housing and social services, so police aren't answering all the calls related to poverty, mental health, homelessness and addictions.

Why Bligh and not Fry?

Bligh says she is grateful for the “cross-partisan” support shown by Ladner, Meggs and Harcourt’s letter.

“For the issues that the city is dealing with every day, I have always gone and sourced out people who have various opinions and various experiences in dealing with those issues for their input,” she said.

As for them endorsing only four of the six Vote Vancouver council candidates, Bligh said she expected partial slate recommendations to happen during the campaign. (In municipal politics, a “slate” is a political party’s entire group of candidates for council, park board and school board. Vote Vancouver is running six council candidates, three school board trustee candidates and two park board commissioner candidates.)

“We have a great slate. All six council candidates have both worked incredibly hard and earned their place on our slate,” she said. “We continue to support them wholeheartedly.”

Like Bligh, Vancouver Greens mayoral candidate Fry has also been on city council since 2018. Asked why they supported Bligh over Fry, Harcourt, Meggs and Ladner cited Fry’s voting record.

They took issue in particular with the number of times Fry abstained from voting this term, noting a potential mayor should be making a yes or no decision on most council votes.

While councillors may abstain as a protest or to excuse themselves from a conflict of interest, under the Vancouver Charter abstention votes are considered a vote in favour.

In total Fry has abstained from 120 votes since he was initially elected to council in 2018, 80 of which have taken place since the Oct, 15, 2022, election. Bligh has abstained from 78 votes since 2018, and 31 of those abstentions happened over the past four-year term on council.

Fry’s abstentions are part of why an article in Spacing magazine in August found that among four opposition councillors, including Bligh, OneCity’s Maloney and COPE’s Sean Orr, Fry was found to have voted with the majority ABC Vancouver councillors most often at 87 per cent, when the magazine examined 50 significant council votes since the April 2025 byelection.

But Bligh was not far behind, voting with ABC councillors 86 per cent of the time.

“I don’t think he’s got it, got the capacity even close to what Rebecca has to be a good mayor, to bring people together, to work co-operatively with other governments — federal and provincial — on the key issues,” Harcourt said of Fry.

“And I think she’ll be able to have a mixed council and has the personal qualities and the temperament to be able to pull people together to work towards common cause and the key issues for a lot of Vancouverites.”

‘As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law.’

President Trump has launched a probe into Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook over mortgage fraud allegations, the White House announced Friday. The move appears aimed at removing Cook from the post following an unfavorable Supreme Court ruling on the matter earlier this year.

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in Friday’s presidential memoranda.

The directive establishes a committee comprised of the president’s assistant for economic policy, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission chair, and the director of the Office of Government Ethics that will investigate allegations that Cook, a Biden appointee, “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.” The group will subsequently report to the president “whether there is ’cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal within the meaning” of federal law “as construed” in the Supreme Court’s Trump v. Cook (2026) decision.

Trump first sought to fire Cook over these allegations in August 2025, but was blocked by D.C. District Judge Jib Cobb, a Biden appointee. The administration ultimately filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to temporarily permit Cook’s removal while litigation over her firing continued. The high court rejected the government’s request in Trump v. Cook.

Writing for the 5-4 majority, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled there must be “cause” to fire Cook, and she must be afforded an “opportunity to respond to the charges made against her … [before] a final decision [can] be made.” The majority declined to rule on “the ultimate question” of whether Trump can remove Cook “for cause,” arguing such a decision “will depend in part on the underlying facts” that must first “be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.”

The court’s decision prompted stinging dissents from Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito (joined by Neil Gorsuch), and Amy Coney Barrett. Thomas noted “[a]pparent mortgage fraud was a ’cause’ to remove Cook” and underscored a point he raised during oral arguments — that “the statute authorizing the President to remove Cook for ’cause’ says nothing about notice or a hearing, so it does not require notice and a hearing.” The senior justice also argued the federal courts lack the authority to “enter the relief” the Cook majority upheld with its decision and further admonished the majority for infringing on the president’s executive removal powers.

Alito (and Gorsuch) argued that Trump showed a likelihood of success on the preliminary questions of whether “for cause” removal applies to pre-office conduct and whether he violated Cook’s due process rights. Meanwhile, Barrett blasted the majority for deciding significant legal matters that had not been fully briefed or contested, as well as the “disconnect between its holding and its disposition line.”

[READ: John Roberts: Presidents Have Executive Power. Also John Roberts: No, They Don’t]

Following the constraints established in Cook, Trump has directed the newly formed committee to “conduct an in-person hearing to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook” on Nov. 5. The hearing will last “no longer than 4 hours,” according to the memoranda.

The directive also grants Cook the ability to file a written statement with the committee contesting the allegations, so long as it is submitted at least three days in advance. While the Biden appointee will be given the opportunity to “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations,” the committee will be afforded the chance to “question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning.”

Cook and her team will be presented the evidence against her prior to the hearing. The committee may also request Cook turn over “documents or other evidentiary submissions … as appropriate,” which Cook is instructed to comply with. The hearing will not be broadcast to the public “but shall be transcribed,” according to the directive.
