Australia's Izzi Batt-Doyle took more than two minutes off her personal best, finishing sixth in the women's race at the Chicago Marathon. (Supplied: Jan Figueroa)

Adelaide runner Izzi Batt-Doyle lowered her own personal best by more than two minutes, breaking the Australian women's marathon record in Chicago.

Her time of 2:20:38 took 46 seconds off the existing record, held by Jess Stenson.

Batt-Doyle, who was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks, finished sixth in the women's race at the Chicago Marathon behind winner Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia.

Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.

Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.

It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.

"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.

"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."

Tigst Assefa ran the final two kilometres of the Berlin Marathon with a badly damaged Achilles tendon, which required immediate surgery to repair. She still ran the third-fastest women's marathon in history.

Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.

"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.

"You don't have masses of people in groups."

Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.

"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.

"The gun went off and second kilometre it was just the two of us, because we were running between groups.

"I spent most of the race trusting our plan and the pacing strategy we had hoped to run the first half in, and hope that I would feel strong in the second half."

Batt-Doyle's race was a model of control, with her splits barely moving. Every 5km block landed between 16:36 and 16:47, holding her at about 3:19 to 3:21 per kilometre from the opening kilometres to the final stretch.

Marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge has time to slow down and wave at the crowds at the MCG and still break the race record at the Melbourne Marathon.

She went through halfway in 1:10:29 and then ran the second half in about 1:10:09, giving her a 20-second negative split.

"We went through halfway in under the time needed to run 2:21, but I wasn't sure because I felt like I was slowing in the second half as it was warmer, and just the general fatigue of the marathon," Batt-Doyle said.

"It was quite warm and we knew going into this week that it was going to be a bit warmer than ideal marathon conditions, but we did what we could do to prepare for that.

"That's hydrating a lot beforehand, and every opportunity that there were water cups I was splashing three or four water cups to keep cool."

But Batt-Doyle didn't fade in the conditions, with her quickest 5km split of 16:36 coming between 35km and 40km. She covered the last 2.2km at about 3:14 per kilometre, when she started to sense the record was hers.

"There is a small hill about 400 to go, and then you turn into the last 150 metres, and I saw the clock and that's when I really started celebrating," she said.

"It was quite emotional. You can think you can do it and hope you can do it, and be on pace to do it, but there is so much that can happen in the last 5 kilometres, or last 1 kilometre or even the last 400 metres.

Batt-Doyle said she was proud to join the list of previous Australian record-holders that included Stenson, Sinead Diver and Benita Willis.

"I think it's really validating for the hard work I've put in and it feels really special to be part of history, because there have been some fantastic runners before me, and fantastic runners to come," she said.

"I really feel honoured, that sums it up. To be in that class of athletes. I'm really proud of that."

Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09.

Here are some questions for reporters to ask New York City’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani at his next news conference. They might help clarify his statement on Oct. 7, 2023, which hijacked the memory of the murders of innocent Israelis so he could bang the drum for his favorite cause.

Perhaps he was simply misunderstood. These questions would help us get a better sense of how the Mayor really feels. Here goes:

“Mayor Mamdani, your wife has used social media to approve of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Jewish civilians, including women, children, and babies. Would you have allowed her to serve as a human shield at Hamas military installments during the Gaza War?”

MAMDANI WROTE AN OCT. 7 STATEMENT. HE ERASED THE JEWS

The question is pertinent because Hamas stationed its military inside densely populated civilian areas, including alongside or inside schools, hospitals, and religious institutions. Hamas also “suggested” to Gazans that they ignore Israeli warnings to evacuate areas about to come under attack. They made those “suggestions” because they cynically desired civilians to get killed, tilting the world’s feelings against Israel.

So the question is whether the mayor would have encouraged his wife to sacrifice herself in the same manner that Hamas sacrificed its civilians. If not, then the two of them are just as cynical about the deaths of Palestinian noncombatants as Hamas itself.

Next question: “Mr. Mayor, you’ve expressed deep concern for the welfare of the Palestinians living in Gaza. Do you have any comment about the great financial wealth of their leadership?”

The Palestinian people have lived in forced poverty for generations while their leaders have accumulated generational wealth. The leader of the Palestinian Authority, Mahmoud Abbas, is said to be worth between $100 million and $600 million. Many of Hamas’s leaders don’t even live in Gaza. They mostly live in wealthy Gulf nations like Qatar. Several are billionaires. The U.S. government estimates that Hamas controls more than $500 million in investments.

Hamas leader Yahyah Sinwar was reportedly a multi-millionaire. When he was killed in the war, he was carrying $11,000. The average monthly pre-war income in Gaza was under $500, which meant that a Gazan would have to work for 22 years (and spend nothing) to accumulate that much cash. His wife was seen carrying a Birkin bag, a coveted Hermes handbag that costs $22,000, when she was headed into a tunnel during the war. A typical Gazan would have to work for 44 years (and spend nothing) to afford a bag like that.

This is nothing new. In 2003, the International Monetary Fund identified $900 million in the personal possession of PLO founder Yassir Arafat. Little of the wealth of these leaders or organizations has ever trickled down to the citizenry of Gaza, where the pre-October 7 unemployment was as high as 64%. It would be great to have the mayor explain why none of this fabulous wealth has been used to improve the lives of Gaza residents.

“Mr. Mayor, you have expressed sympathy for the Israelis taken hostage. Are you planning to honor the Gazans who voluntarily stepped forward to tell journalists, U.N. workers, or IDF members where any of the hostages were being held?”

OK, this is a trick question. No such people have ever been identified.

“Mr. Mayor, some members of the gay community in New York have advocated strenuously on behalf of Gaza during the war. Have you advocated for gay rights with Gaza’s leaders, or are you comfortable with the fact that queer people are thrown from the rooftops of buildings because of their sexual identity?”

Admittedly, a leading question. There is plenty of evidence of lethal behavior toward LGBT people on the part of Gaza’s leadership, but there is no evidence that Mayor Mamdani has ever sought to shift attitudes or behaviors toward gays anywhere in the Middle East.

“Mr. Mayor, millions of Palestinians live in poverty in refugee camps. Have you urged Arab nations throughout the Middle East to take them in?”

MAMDANI’S OCT. 7 STATEMENT ISN’T PRO-PALESTINIAN. IT’S PRO-HAMAS

Admittedly, the problems surrounding Palestinian refugees are difficult, perhaps too difficult even for the Mayor of New York to resolve, despite his ongoing interest in international affairs. But perhaps he might have a word with the leaders of the almost two dozen Arab-majority countries around the world. He could seek to persuade them to give housing, jobs, and education to the refugees while their legal situation is adjudicated. Who knows? He might even win the Nobel Peace Prize before his friend, President Donald Trump.

In short, “Free Gaza” is a statement that everyone can get behind. Gaza needs to be freed from its corrupt leadership if its people are ever to have a chance of a better life.

putting-a-ring-on-it-london-tree-ring:
Ten million people stand to benefit from a cooler and more biodiverse capital, say the organisers of an ambitious project to reconnect its wilder spaces

Ten million people stand to benefit from a cooler and more biodiverse capital, say the organisers of an ambitious project to reconnect its wilder spaces

“An M25 for nature”: that’s how the brains behind the London Tree Ring describe their plan to encircle the capital with a 200km (124 mile) green corridor weaving along the boundaries of its outer boroughs.

The project, from the charity, CPRE London, is designed to safeguard greenbelt, boost biodiversity in neglected pockets of woodland, and return all-but vanished species to London’s treescapes.

And people are at the heart of the plan, they say. Over the next 25 years, community groups, schools, skills providers and landowners are being invited to find new sites, plant trees and care for green spaces.

“It’s that community buy-in: working with local people with a vested interest, who get to follow the trees from seed to maturity,” said London Tree Ring director Phil Paulo. “In return, there’s a whole range of benefits that trees will bring, from urban cooling to fixing carbon to community orchards.”

The idea has been gathering momentum since 2023, but gets an official launch on 15 October following years of research and a handful of test runs at showcase sites.

In one example, on London’s south-west border, the project worked with a countryside skills provider to revive hedgerows by planting 1,500 trees, including disease-resistant elm. The species was almost wiped out in the 60s and 70s, but is the sole food source for caterpillars of the white-letter hairstreak butterfly, whose populations have since fallen by 80%.

“We’re bringing back a tree lost from our landscape due to Dutch elm disease,” said Paulo, “and we’re looking at where else we can use trees to address species and habitat loss.”

Meanwhile in Sutton, CPRE London teamed up with council tree wardens and children from Glenthorne high school, to create a ‘Miyawake’ microforest at Reigate Avenue recreation ground. The Japanese method involves densely planting native trees into fungi-enriched soil to boost nutrient uptake.

“Despite these dry conditions, it’s established really well with limited irrigation,” Paulo explained. “Everyone’s aware of the issues we’ve had this summer with drought, water availability and fire, so it’s thinking about what species will be adaptable … trees that can provide us with shade.”

It’s that community buy-in: working with local people with a vested interest, who get to follow the trees from seed to maturity

CPRE London is already working with partners including the Forestry Commission, Woodland Trust and Trees for Cities. In time, Paulo believes the project can grow into a city-wide movement, inspiring hundreds more community groups and volunteers to help restore London’s green edge.“

And this isn’t just about London,” he added. “As a national charity, we’ll be sharing what we learn across the CPRE family, so it can be replicated in other cities, towns and green belt areas across the UK.

The 22-year-old Massachusetts man arrested in Vermont Thursday hours after his mother was found shot dead in her kitchen has waived extradition and agreed to be returned to his home state.

Ryan Hanafin was the subject of an interstate manhunt Thursday after his 48-year-old father Matthew Hanafin arrived home around 12:38 a.m. and found his wife, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin, shot dead in their kitchen in Reading, Massachusetts, according to Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan.

The local prosecutor said in court that she had spoken with Massachusetts State Police and expected them to be able to retrieve Ryan Hanafin “pretty quickly” in a brief hearing Friday afternoon.

In a hearing where both the judge and defendant appeared virtually, with only the lawyers and media in the courtroom, Hanafin answered “Yes sir,” when asked if he could hear the judge.

Hanafin was wearing a blue protective covering over his chest and shoulders as he appeared remotely.

“You are charged with crimes, felony crimes, in the state of Massachusetts, and they would like to have you returned,” the judge said. “You have the right to go through what is called the formal governor’s warrant process, and that’s where the governor of Massachusetts formally asks the governor of Vermont to surrender you, and that takes some time, and they have to make sure that their paperwork is correct, then they would send you back.”

The judge added that he could file a habeas petition and challenge the state’s authority to hold him in the meantime.

“The most common basis for that might be that you were the wrong Ryan Hanafin,” the judge said. “By waiving extradition, you’re giving up your opportunity to go through the governor’s warrant process and file any habeas petition. Do you understand that?”

“Yes sir,” Hanafin replied.

The judge asked if he had taken any drugs or had any mental conditions that would affect his judgment or make it difficult to understand the proceedings.

“No sir,” Hanafin replied to each question.

He said he had spoken with his attorney and understood his advice.

“All right,” the judge continued, “is it your voluntary choice to waive extradition and return to Massachusetts?”

“Yes, that’s what I’d like to do,” Hanafin replied.

Timing for his return to Massachusetts to face charges in Reading, where his mother was shot to death, was not immediately clear.

The judge set a status conference for next Thursday to make sure Hanafin’s transfer had been completed.

“We’ll set it for status next Thursday just to make sure Massachusetts has retrieved him, and if they haven’t yet, we’ll ask for some status report on that,” he said.

The entire hearing lasted roughly four minutes.

Reading police have so far called him a person of interest and not a suspect, and authorities have not publicly identified the Massachusetts felony charges referenced during Friday’s extradition hearing.

Vermont state troopers were on the lookout for his black Dodge Charger in Warren, Vermont, where he had known ties.

About two hours into their search, they found him, and he was arrested without incident, authorities said.
16-cozy-activities-to-add-to-your-fall-b:
By

Malaka Gharib

,

Clare Marie Schneider

,

Marielle Segarra

One clever way to celebrate the season? Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.
                
                    
                    Hannah Churn for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.

Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook, shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup: a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days.

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta.

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person? Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."

If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions.)

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste, says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month. "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit, she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."

Create a home theater. Devika Girish, co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine, explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.

Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto, likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks, says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity. If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.

Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours.

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta.

Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering. Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.

Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari, a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions, shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.

Our partner Rob Brezsny, whose latest book is Enlightenment for Rebels: Celebrating Our Wild and Sacred Earthly Selves, provides his weekly wisdom to enlighten our thinking and motivate our mood. Rob’s Free Will Astrology, is a syndicated weekly column appearing in over a hundred publications. He is also the author of Pronoia Is the Antidote for Paranoia: How All of Creation Is Conspiring To Shower You with Blessings. (A free preview of the book is available here.)

Here is your weekly horoscope…

FREE WILL ASTROLOGY – Week of October 10, 2026
Copyright by Rob Brezsny, FreeWillAstrology.com

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22):
Periodically, you have the cosmic right to receive precisely what you need. Life is duty-bound to deliver a close approximation of full satisfaction. I believe now is one of those times. So please be bold and articulate about naming the specific blessings you require. Write them down, speak them aloud, and pray for them—not as a demand, but as a hearty invitation. Then, for a while, live as if all of creation is indeed honor-bound to respond accordingly, adjusting its behavior so it’s in harmony with the gifts you’ve asked for.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21):
Every Thursday night, I haul my trash bin out to the street so the collectors can empty it the following morning. Most weeks it’s three-quarters full. But now and then I produce an unusually large haul of debris. On those occasions, I have to turn into a one-person compaction crew: I grab a low-hanging branch of the persimmon tree, hoist myself up, drop down feet-first into the can, and bounce around to squash everything enough to squeeze in the overflow. Consider this my audition to be your role model, Scorpio. According to my reading of the celestial weather, it’s time for you to consolidate and discard at least half a year’s accumulation of obsolete clutter—both the invisible emotional kind and the tangible stuff filling your space.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21):
Ancient navigators sometimes crossed vast stretches of sea by studying the swells beneath their boats. Their bodies were instruments of perception that enabled them to feel the subtle wave patterns generated by winds and distant islands. Your intuition has a similar sensitivity these days, Sagittarius. I hope you will trust it: what your whole being senses before your rational mind assembles the evidence. I call this fully embodied intelligence. It deserves a key role in your decision-making.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19):
I’ve never been a fan of Capricorn poet Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931). The ideas he expressed seem commonplace and sentimental to me. But his book The Prophet is an all-time bestseller translated into over 100 languages. Millions of readers have adored and benefited from his words, and he’s acclaimed as a literary hero in his native Lebanon. So who cares what I think! I’ll just shut up and appreciate the fact that he worked hard and published a lot. His disciplined, painstaking efforts have been widely inspirational. Let’s make him your role model for the coming months. I think you’re primed to create enduring offerings that nourish people’s souls.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18):
Think of an aspect of your life that you have always wished you could change but have assumed or feared you could never change. What if, sometime soon, you try to change it, but this time you do it with playful lightheartedness? You resolve to feel zero stress and have as much fun as possible as you try to shift how this problem works. You decide you will use your imagination to dream up unprecedented and even outrageous ways to break your trance and invite sweet liberation to swoop in.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20):
Geologists tell us that over time, rocks really do get transformed under sustained pressure. Their material gets reorganized into denser, more stable stuff. This is an apt metaphor for you, dear Pisces. You’re under pressure right now, and it may feel intense. But what if it’s actually reconfiguring you? Maybe the constraints are what you need to make you more focused, more essential, and more real. Not all pressure is bad, and this is proof. Ask yourself: What is this pressure making possible that freedom couldn’t create? Let yourself be reorganized.

ARIES (March 21-April 19):
“Dear Oracle: My secret terror is being ordinary. I need to be special, and lately I’m worried I’m just average and unremarkable. That thought is repugnant to me! Can you offer any advice? —Afraid of Average”… Dear Afraid: The pressure to be extraordinary is exhausting because it’s the wrong goal. Your birthright and your life assignment aren’t about being special in the sense of better-than. You’re simply meant to be vividly, generously, amazingly yourself. In the coming weeks, I invite you to trade the anxious hunt for superiority for the warm, throbbing joy of full self-expression. Shine because it feels fantastic, not to outrank anyone.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20):
Ravens sometimes hide food while pretending to conceal it elsewhere, especially if another raven is observing. They’re strategic and imaginative and aware of how they’re perceived. With their social intelligence as inspiration, I will encourage you to think more consciously about the stories you’re broadcasting. Which precious projects will flourish better if protected from premature scrutiny? Do you have any in-progress blooms that really should continue to incubate before being revealed? Discernment isn’t deception. PS: Conversely, there may be a part of you that deserves greater visibility.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20):
The Taurus philosopher Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life must be lived forward but can only be understood backward. You Geminis are naturally inclined to resist that advice. Many of you analyze experiences while they’re still unfolding. Can I coax you to try a different approach in the coming weeks? As usual, you may be tempted to figure everything out immediately. But the most useful clarity won’t arrive until later, as you survey what has occurred and recognize patterns you couldn’t see in real time. So try to stay curious rather than overly diagnostic. Keep gathering impressions, stories, and clues. Allow events to transpire like chapters in a book whose ending you haven’t reached yet.

CANCER (June 21-July 22):
The Germans have a word, Sehnsucht, for a feeling that my English language can’t quite convey: a deep, sweet, aching longing for something you can’t name. It may be a faraway home you’ve never visited or a wholeness you seem to remember without ever having had it. Most people treat this yearning as a problem to be fixed or numbed. But I think it’s sacred information, Cancerian, and you’re especially fluent in it right now. Don’t rush to resolve the ache or explain it away. Instead, follow it like a scent. What is your Sehnsucht pointing toward? Let it lead you toward the beauty and meaning your soul is homesick for.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22):
Botanists know that climbing vines have a simple approach. They keep extending their sensitive tendrils until they discover something sturdy enough to support upward growth. Their progress depends on continual experimentation. I love it when you imitate this style of intelligence, Leo, which I think will be especially useful and successful during the coming weeks. So instead of demanding guarantees before beginning a new endeavor, offer exploratory feelers. Ask friendly questions. Test prototypes. The right support system probably already exists, but may not reveal itself until you reach toward it.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22):
One of my favorite Virgos works in a museum cleaning centuries-old paintings with exquisite patience. She uses tiny swabs and gentle solvents to lift away layers of darkened varnish and grime. She’s an expert at making the original colors emerge so vividly that the painting looks newly made. But her work demands artful restraint. If she presses too hard or applies the wrong solvent, she could destroy the very thing she means to reveal. This approach can be your specialty in the coming weeks, Virgo. I hope you will attend to valuables that have been obscured by accumulated grime, like old habits, stale assumptions, and other people’s projections. Your task is to gently lift it all away and let the true colors shine.

autism-adhd-support-before-diagnosis-nhs:
Share article

Print article

I hated myself so much…and now I love myself. I’m not perfect. But I’ve accepted myself now.

That was how one person described the impact of receiving an autism and ADHD diagnosis when my colleagues and I interviewed them about their mental health.

For this participant, finally understanding why they had struggled for so long had transformed how they felt about themselves.

Their experience highlights an important issue as the NHS considers changes to how people receive support for autism and ADHD.

A recently published independent review, commissioned by the government, recommends that people in England should be able to receive help according to their needs without waiting for a formal diagnosis.

This could make an enormous difference to people who currently spend years waiting for an assessment. But while earlier support is welcome, diagnosis can have benefits that go far beyond helping someone access treatment.

Autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are conditions that affect how people experience and respond to the world. Autism can affect communication, social interaction and how someone experiences their surroundings. ADHD can affect attention, organisation and the ability to control impulses. Both vary considerably from person to person.

Demand for assessments has increased dramatically. By the end of 2025, more than 560,000 ADHD referrals and 254,000 autism referrals remained open in England.

These growing waiting lists mean people can struggle for years without understanding their difficulties or receiving appropriate help.

Mental health problems are also common among autistic people and those with ADHD. These can include anxiety, which involves excessive worry or fear, and depression, which can cause prolonged low mood and a loss of interest in everyday activities.

Providing support before diagnosis could help people who are struggling now, rather than leaving them waiting until their difficulties become more severe.

As part of MINDS (Mental Illness, Neurodivergence and Distress) a research project investigating how autistic adults and people with ADHD experience mental health difficulties and access care – my colleagues and I interviewed 25 adults who were autistic, had ADHD or had both conditions. We asked about their experiences of getting mental health support through their GP surgeries.

Participants described how receiving a diagnosis helped them understand experiences they had previously blamed themselves for. Some had spent years struggling, without knowing why.

For others, diagnosis provided a way to explain their needs to friends, family and healthcare professionals. It also helped them find approaches that made everyday life easier.

These experiences show how diagnosis can improve someone’s understanding and acceptance of themselves, particularly after years of confusion or self-criticism.

The government review acknowledges these benefits and recommends that assessments should remain available. However, there is a risk that overstretched NHS services could increasingly restrict access to them.

In West Yorkshire, for example, a minimum two-year wait has been introduced for routine autism and ADHD assessments carried out by independent providers through the NHS. People with urgent needs may be assessed sooner.

Offering support without a diagnosis could ease some of the pressure on these services. But it should not become a reason to make assessments harder to obtain.

Our research also revealed that receiving a diagnosis did not necessarily mean people could access suitable mental health care.

Many participants described difficulties getting help from their GP surgery. Some struggled to explain what they were experiencing or understand whether their difficulties were related to autism, ADHD or a separate mental health problem.

Others felt that healthcare professionals did not fully understand their experiences.

Several described being referred from one service to another, only to be turned away because their needs were considered too complicated or because they were not unwell enough to qualify for help.

Some participants were offered cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a talking therapy that helps people recognise and change patterns of thinking and behaviour that contribute to emotional distress.

Although CBT can help autistic people and those with ADHD, some participants found particular techniques unsuitable. A few said the treatment made them feel worse.

One autistic participant described how repeatedly facing situations that caused anxiety, an approach sometimes used in therapy, felt like an “assault” on their nervous system.

For some autistic people, distress can be linked to overwhelming sensory experiences, such as loud noises or bright lights. Therapy may need to take these differences into account.

National treatment guidance already recommends adapting talking therapies to meet autistic adults’ needs. But our findings suggest that in addition to adapting therapies, we need to provide a different kind of support to address a wider range of needs.

Years of unsuccessful attempts to get help had left some participants feeling abandoned.

GP surgeries already provide mental health support to many autistic people and people with ADHD. If more people become eligible for help without a diagnosis, demand on these services could increase further.

GPs will need sufficient time, training and resources to understand people’s needs and help them find appropriate support.

The government’s proposal offers an opportunity to improve care, particularly for people who currently face long waits. But its success will depend on whether services can provide suitable help, both before and after diagnosis.

For some people, diagnosis can transform how they understand themselves. Others urgently need practical help or treatment for their mental health. Many need both.

As one participant described the experience of finally receiving a diagnosis but finding little support afterwards:

You just get to the end of the diagnosis and then you fall off a cliff. It’s a bit like a conveyor belt in a supermarket without a trolley at the end.

The challenge now is to ensure that people receive the help they need while waiting for an assessment, and continue receiving appropriate support afterwards.

Lecturer in Primary Care Mental Health, University of Southampton

federal-judge-bars-group-fencing-colorad:
The Colorado Sun

Telling stories that matter in a dynamic, evolving state.

A federal judge has permanently barred a group from fencing off about 1,400 acres of U.S. Forest Service land outside Mancos, ruling that the group has no legal claim to the public land in the San Juan National Forest.

U.S. District Court Judge Daniel D. Domenico ruled Sept. 30 that the Free Land Holder Committee and its two representatives, Patrick Pipkin and Bryan Hammon, cannot install another fence or obstruct public access to the property.

The ruling comes two years after the group began hanging signs around the Four Corners region to stake their claim to the land under the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the war between Mexico and the United States with Mexico ceding about half of its territory. The group also installed a barbed wire fence around the land.

The fence ignited a dispute with local residents, who called it an “outright theft” of public land used for hiking, biking, grazing and hunting. Residents, with tools in hand, dismantled the fence shortly after it went up, while Montezuma County Sheriff Steve Nowlin and deputies stood by to document the incident and keep the peace.

In his 12-page ruling, Domenico wrote that the government’s evidence established its ownership of the land and that the group’s posted notices and proclamations do not give them any right to fence or prevent the public or livestock from accessing the land.

Government attorneys “properly supported facts, which are considered undisputed, demonstrate that the United States owns the Hallar Deed Area as a matter of law,” Domenico wrote Sept. 30. “Mr. Pipkin’s and Mr. Hammon’s asserted chain of publicly posted notices, proclamations, and the like does not have legal force and does not establish they they or the Free Land Holder Committee have ‘title by nature,’ a good-faith claim to or ‘color of title,’ ‘exclusive beneficial use,’ or any other right to fence, inclose, exclude others from, or obstruct the free passage of people or livestock over any part of the Hallard Deed Area.”

The judge also noted that Pipkin and Hammon had missed court deadlines for responding to the government’s motion for judgment.

The federal government filed a lawsuit in November 2024, asking a judge to prevent the group from fencing off the land. Nowlin said at the time that the dispute should be resolved by a judge, noting that his authority did not extend to resolving civil disputes over federal land. The group agreed to pause further fence construction while the case proceeded.

The property, known as the Hallar Deed Area, was once privately owned through claims under the Homestead Act. The federal government reacquired it in 1927 after owner Fred Hallar offered the land in exchange for timber. One reason the Forest Service sought to acquire the property was to protect the watershed, court records stated.

In a 2024 interview, Pipkin told The Sun he is Native American and his group has Native American members who trace their presence on the property back “before there was a United States.” He declined to mention the tribes he was working with.

The Free Land Holder Committee’s argument in court documents focused on the capitalization of “the” in historical references to the United States. Pipkin argued that the Founding Fathers established the country as “The United States of America,” with a capital “T.” But as other documents were signed as “the United States of America, it created a separate entity.

The court record includes an unusual exchange following a February 2025 status conference, when Pipkin, who asked to be referred to as “The Man Patrick,” left 12 silver coins with a courtroom deputy despite the judge’s warning that the court could not accept them as payment for filing fees. The coins, each weighing 1 troy ounce, were valued at about $377 at the time, according to the court. Because the court could not process them as payment, the coins were placed in the finance department’s vault until Pipkin could retrieve them.

Pipkin and Hammon represented themselves in the case and did not immediately respond to emails from The Colorado Sun seeking comment about their plans for the land.

Both filed responses this week asking Domenico to amend his ruling, according to court records.

Meta has banned ads from TikTok’s Chinese parent company ByteDance across the US and several other countries as the rivalry between the major social media operators heats up, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The ban, which went into effect on Thursday, restricts ads and paid marketing messages from ByteDance, along with third-party ads that link to TikTok.

“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Christopher Sgro said in a statement to The Verge. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”

The move comes just months after Meta agreed to a major child safety settlement, requiring it to pay $17 billion and add new restrictions for teens. Meta has since called on TikTok and YouTube to impose similar safeguards, including by waging an ad campaign that TikTok reportedly declined to share on its platform. TikTok has also stopped allowing users to include links that “open or log you into other social media apps,” according to its support page

Though TikTok in the US is now controlled by a joint venture majority-owned by US-based companies, ByteDance remains a major shareholder. In addition to pulling TikTok ads in the US, the policy will also restrict them in Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

hurricane_isaias_2026:
(AP) - A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.

For now, it’s the waters charged by climate change.

All Atlantic hurricane season there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.

El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.

It’s called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany’s Kristen Corbosiero said.

The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather.

“But there’s a certain point where it’s like, I don’t care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win,” Klotzbach said.

The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn’t quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño’s high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm’s top sideways, experts said.

Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions.

Wind shear wasn’t exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said.

“The warm waters and high moisture won,” Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said.

By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall.

Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said.

But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in “a tenuous spot” because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said.

“Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change,” Dahl said. “So in this part of the world, there’s been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that’s attributable directly to climate change.”

The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge “life-threatening.”

A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend.

“There’s a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño’s like a little icing on the cake,” Dahl said.

As the attendees sat at the edge of their seats waiting to hear the fate of the people whose stories were told, a fire alarm went off, disrupting the evening.

Ann McElhinney, who co-wrote the play "OCTOBER 7" with her husband, Phelim McAleer, told Fox News Digital that many audience members initially remained seated, believing the alarms were part of the show.

"Initially, they thought it was part of the play because they heard these sirens going off, and the dialogue prior to that had been about sirens going off, rockets going off, the red alarm going off," McElhinney explained to Fox News Digital. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

Cahn Auditorium was evacuated when someone pulled a fire alarm during a performance of the play "OCTOBER 7" on Oct. 6, 2026. ("OCTOBER 7 THE PLAY")

After the theater had been evacuated and cleared by authorities, many people left, according to McElhinney, who told Fox News Digital that she believed that people were scared by the incident. However, she said others who chose to stay, feeling "defiant" and refusing "to be terrified by this."

McAleer noted that the performance ended with a standing ovation, which he believed was both a tribute to those who worked on the show and those who returned after the alarm went off.

"The standing ovation was for the actors, the standing ovation was for the director, the standing ovation was for the stories. But it's also, I think people were giving themselves a standing ovation that someone had tried to intimidate them, that someone had tried to say to them, 'You're not going to tell the truth. We don't want to hear the truth, we want to shut you up, we want to shut down, we want to frighten you and intimidate you.' And they didn't succeed," McAleer told Fox News Digital.

The event continued as planned and concluded at 9:45 p.m. The Northwestern University Police Department will continue their investigation."

Actors in "OCTOBER 7" at Northwestern University tell the stories of those who were impacted by the 2023 Hamas attacks in Israel. ("OCTOBER 7 THE PLAY")

The couple said they believe someone deliberately activated the fire alarm after sitting through much of the performance.

"This was someone, we believe, someone sat through the play and then came out at the most emotional time," McAleer told Fox News Digital.

"It's something very insidious that someone decided to disrupt this rather than even, by the way, have a protest, make their voice heard. Husband and wife team Ann McElhinney and Phelim McAleer participate in a question-and-answer session after their play was put on at Northwestern University. ("OCTOBER 7 THE PLAY")

"That tells you something about free speech in New York City," McElhinney said. She pointed out that the play, which focuses on the experiences of Israelis, including Jewish survivors of the attacks, needed security while being performed in a city with a large Jewish population.

MIKE WALTZ FIGHTS BACK TEARS REVEALING WHAT HAMAS HOSTAGE REFUSED TO DO BEFORE RELEASE

zelensky-poland-honour-row:
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has been stripped of Poland's highest state honour, the Order of the White Eagle, over Kyiv's decision to name a military unit after controversial World War Two fighters.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki branded Ukraine's decision late last month to name the unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) "outrageous",  "incomprehensible" and "deeply disappointing".

Nawrocki stressed the diplomatic row would not impact Poland's support for Ukraine against Russia.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha denounced Warsaw's move, calling it a "strategic mistake" and "disrespectful".

Many in Ukraine regard the UPA, which existed in the 1940s and 1950s, as heroes who fought for Ukrainian independence against the Soviet Red Army as well as Nazi Germany and Polish authorities. So for Ukrainians the title "Heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army" is a major honour.

Poland, however, accuses the UPA of carrying out a genocide of ethnic Poles in Volhynia (now Volyn in Ukraine) in 1943-45.

"For the overwhelming majority of Polish society, the UPA remains, above all, a formation responsible for the brutal crimes committed against citizens of the Republic of Poland during World War II," Nawrocki said in a video released on the president's official website.

"That is why the Ukrainian authorities' decision to glorify the UPA is not only outrageous, it is also incomprehensible and deeply disappointing," he said.

"It hurts not only our historical memory. It also undermines the trust built up over the years and in recent months," he added.

The Polish president pointed to the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees welcomed into the country following the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

"Poles opened their borders, their homes, and their hearts to millions of Ukrainians," he said.

He went on to say: "Ukraine's path toward European structures also requires a willingness to honestly confront the difficult chapters of its own history.

"A united Europe was built on the rejection of totalitarianism and the cult of violence. These principles must apply to everyone. For those who do not understand this, there can be no place in the European Union, and Poland will certainly not allow it."

Ukraine has ambitions to become an EU member state and attended the first phase of membership negotiations this week in Luxembourg.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has attempted to dampen growing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw.

Taking to social media on Friday, the former president of the European Council said the feud "delights" Russia's Vladimir Putin and called on Zelensky and Nawrocki to "calm emotions, not to stoke tensions".

For Ukraine, the UPA is a symbol of resistance and struggle for independence, even though Warsaw says about 100,000 ethnic Poles were killed in the Volhynia massacres.

The group's red and black flag is often used by Ukrainian troops on the front line today. That's why Zelensky said he would use the UPA's name for a military unit, "with the aim of restoring the historical traditions of the national army".

The Polish Order of the White Eagle was bestowed on Zelensky in 2023 by then-President Andrzej Duda.

Zelensky himself has not directly commented on the row. But Sybiha called it "a strategic mistake by the President of Poland, from which only Moscow benefits".

He said as a result of the announcement, he would be returning an award he received from Poland in 2022.

"No president of another country will dictate our history to us," he said.

zelenskyy_putin_g20_miami:
OTTAWA — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin if the Russian leader is invited by the United States to attend the G20 summit in Miami later this year.

“Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” Zelenskyy told German broadcaster DW at Canadian Forces Base North Bay on Friday.

In the interview, published Saturday during Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada, the Ukrainian president said the nature of any exchange with Putin was less important than its outcome.

“Results matter. That's it,” he said.

Zelenskyy and Putin have met in person only once, during a Normandy format summit in Paris in December 2019.

Responding to Zelenskyy’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov pointed to Putin’s previous suggestion that the Ukrainian leader could travel to Russia for talks.

“If he really wants to meet with Putin, Putin has previously said that he can fly to Moscow,” Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass.

The 2026 G20 summit is scheduled to take place in Miami, Florida, on Dec. 14-15. Putin last attended a G20 summit in person in 2019, although he participated by videoconference in 2020 and 2021.

Zelenskyy also outlined Ukraine’s air defense needs ahead of winter, saying Kyiv is seeking to secure between 100 and 120 interceptor missiles per month.

He claimed Russia is currently producing 140 ballistic missiles a month and said that, based on NATO standards, intercepting that number would require twice as many defensive missiles.

“You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it's a huge challenge to have even 100 missiles per month,” Zelenskyy said.

He said Ukraine could obtain the missiles from US stockpiles or production and was also discussing potential supplies with countries in the Middle East, without identifying them or providing details of the talks.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine also aims to receive and test the first prototype of FREYJA, a pan-European anti-ballistic missile defense project initiated by Kyiv earlier this year, by the end of December before moving toward production.
zelensky_peace_conditions:
The leaders of Ukraine and its close European allies - the UK, France and Germany - have set out five conditions for reaching a "just and lasting" deal to end the war with Russia.

In a joint statement after talks in London, Volodymyr Zelensky, UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they would "stand firmly with Ukraine".

The five conditions include a stop to the fighting, starting negotiations from the current position in the field as well as "robust" security guarantees for Ukraine.

The leaders reiterated the need for the US to be part of the process at a time when US President Donald Trump's focus has shifted to the war with Iran.

Back in December, the US pushed Russia and Ukraine to sign up quickly to a plan to end the war, which began with Russian President Vladimir Putin's decision in February 2022 to launch a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The warring sides have recently intensified attacks against each other, with Russia using missiles and drones to attack Ukrainian cities - and Ukraine displaying increased abilities to reach deep into Russian territory with new technology.

On Saturday, Ukrainian drones hit Russia's second-largest city, St Petersburg, as it hosted the final day of a major economic forum - an attack described as "unprecedented" by Russian authorities.

Days earlier, Kyiv had attacked the outskirts of the same city - some 1,000km (620 miles) from Ukraine - as Putin's flagship forum was getting started.

On the eve of the event, Zelensky sent an open letter to Putin calling for direct negotiations to end the war - an offer repeatedly rejected by the Russian leader. Putin said he would end the war only when Russia's goals had been met.

The three Western powers meeting at 10 Downing Street in London on Sunday constitute the so-called E3 group and are some of Kyiv's strongest allies. The UK and France lead the "coalition of the willing" initiative to provide security guarantees for Ukraine as part of any future peace process.

They welcomed Zelensky's letter to Putin and supported his call for "a direct dialogue between Ukraine and Russia - with active US and European participation".

In an apparent reference to Moscow's insistence that Ukraine give up its ambition to join the Nato defence alliance, they said Ukraine right "to choose its own security arrangements and alliances must be fully respected".

Before arriving in London, the Ukrainian leader accused Russia of a "vile" attack after Kyiv officials said a drone had struck a storage facility for spent nuclear fuel near the Chornobyl nuclear plant.

There were no injuries and a fire was put out with radiation levels remaining stable.

Separately, at least three people were killed in a Russian strike in a village outside Zaporizhzhia in the south of the country, authorities said.

Zaporizhzhia has come under relentless Russian attacks recently, with at least two people killed there on Saturday.

The Russian strike on Chornobyl "partially destroyed" a spent nuclear fuel storage building, according to Ukraine's state-owned nuclear operator, Enerhoatom.

The operator said there were no injuries, and a fire in the building was put out, adding that radiation remained at a normal level.

The body also criticised Moscow for what it called a deliberate threat to nuclear safety, in words echoed by Zelensky.

"Russia deliberately struck this particular nuclear infrastructure facility," Zelensky said in a post on X, describing the building as an "as extremely critical infrastructure facility" and the attack as "vile".

Chornobyl - known during the Soviet era as Chernobyl - is the world's worst non-military nuclear disaster. A catastrophic explosion in 1986 sent a plume of radioactive material into the air, triggering a public health emergency across Europe.

Last year, a Russian drone hit the protective shelter over its damaged nuclear reactor.

This means that in the US, Zyn can now assert that “using Zyn instead of cigarettes puts you at a lower risk of mouth cancer, heart disease, lung cancer, stroke, emphysema and chronic bronchitis.”

The decision does not mean nicotine pouches are safe or approved as smoking cessation products. It simply allows Swedish Match, which manufactures Zyn, to market certain products as a less harmful alternative for adults who completely switch away from cigarettes.

The regulatory green light comes at a time wheN the nicotine-pouch boom has already reshaped the conversation about alternatives to smoking. Nicotine pouches have become one of the fastest-growing nicotine categories globally, fueled by their discreet nature, lack of smoke or vapor, and growing perceptions that they represent a “cleaner” form of nicotine consumption.

According to a recent report by the World Health Organization, global retail sales of nicotine pouches reached 23.4 billion units in 2024, an increase of more than 50 percent from the previous year, underscoring just how quickly the category is growing.

The FDA announcement comes as the WHO warns that nicotine pouches are spreading so rapidly that regulation is struggling to keep pace in many countries, and that brands are increasingly using social media, influencers, and youth-oriented marketing to promote them.

It’s the first time regulators have formally endorsed an idea that many younger nicotine users had already embraced. It is not, however, a blessing for the category. In many ways, regulators are simply catching up with a cultural shift that already happened.

The market for smoking alternatives has splintered well beyond the offerings of a decade ago. While nicotine-replacement therapies such as patches, gum, and inhalers remain FDA-approved tools designed to help people quit smoking, they now compete with a rapidly expanding ecosystem of alternative nicotine products.

Oral nicotine pouches have rapidly become one of the biggest growth categories. Zyn and other brands like On! and VELO have become the front-runners in the oral nicotine market globally.

Vapes and disposable e-cigarettes, meanwhile, still take the biggest share of the global smoking-alternative category, projected to hit $14.8 billion by 2030 in the US, even though they’re still dogged by headlines about youth use. Heated tobacco devices, like IQOS, offer another choice by heating tobacco instead of burning it, which lowers exposure to many of the harmful chemicals found in cigarette smoke.

Public health officials remain cautious about nicotine pouches. The WHO has warned that they are becoming increasingly popular among adolescents and young adults because of their “strong youth appeal and high addiction potential,” raising concerns that products initially marketed to smokers could also attract new users.

Based on toxicology data, consumer research, and public health modeling, though, the FDA gave a Modified Risk Tobacco Product (MRTP) order to 10 Zyn flavors at each of two strengths—3 milligrams and 6 milligrams. This allows Swedish Match to market those specific products as a lower-risk alternative for adults who switch completely away from cigarettes.

The new designations are a big win for the tobacco industry, but there are two significant caveats.

First, the ruling only applies to 20 specific products, not all nicotine pouches. Second, the FDA’s findings only apply to smokers who fully switch to these pouches.

Those who use cigarettes or vapes as well as pouches won’t get the same benefit, and the FDA has advised non-tobacco users against using nicotine pouches. “FDA’s review of modified risk products is intended to ensure that adult users have clear, science-based information about the relative harms of tobacco products, so they can make informed choices,” said Bret Koplow, acting director of the FDA’s Center for Tobacco Products. He also stated that the decision “informs adults who smoke about the lower risks associated with these products.” Swedish Match must also keep track of real-world usage and report back to the FDA. The MRTP order is valid for five years, unless it is renewed or withdrawn.

The FDA’s message is relatively straightforward: Adults who smoke and completely switch to certain nicotine pouches are likely reducing their health risks compared to continuing to smoke cigarettes.

But the agency also stresses that there is no safe tobacco product and that fully quitting all tobacco and nicotine products remains the best option for better health. Who ultimately uses nicotine pouches—and whether their rapid growth creates a new generation of nicotine users—is a separate question entirely.

An elderly man was fatally savaged by a pack of dogs on an Illinois road — and a Google Maps search of the scene provides a harrowing result.

James L. Gibson, 68, was attacked by a pack of dogs on the street in Washington Park on Thursday night, Fox 2 reported.

Gibson suffered bite wounds to his face, torso, arms, and legs after he was attacked by at least five dogs while taking a smoke break from working on a rental property, according to local First Alert 4.

The victim was reported dead at the scene, Fox 2 reported.

The outlet claimed that Google Street View images of the scene back in April show the dogs running freely in the street.

Five dogs can be seen roaming down roads amidst homes, a small farm shed, and detached tractor-trailer shipping containers, according to Google Maps.

The Post has not been able to independently verify whether the dogs pictured were involved in the attack.

water-jacket-tech:
A new high tech jacket developed by engineers at the University of Texas can pull drinking water from thin air.

With the advance in fabric technology, the jacket can collect up to one-and-a-half pints of drinkable water a day, say scientists.

They suggest the ground-breaking technology could benefit anyone who spends a lot of time in areas without easy access to drinking water, like hikers, campers, runners, agricultural workers, and soldiers.

“Water harvesting from air is usually imagined as a stationary device such as a box, a panel. We wanted to rethink the form,” said research co-leader Professor Guihua Yu. By focusing on the fibers rather than building another bulky device, the researchers overcame a common problem in the field.

He explained that the textile incorporated into the jacket collects moisture and funnels it to detachable harvesting units, which are then “placed in a foldable collector and heated to produce the water”.

The jacket produced between 400 and 900 milliliters (0.7 to 1.5 pints) of drinkable water per day, depending on humidity levels, according to a study published in the journal Science Advances.

Compared with conventional water-harvesting materials, the textile showed a three- to 10-fold improvement at scale.

“The important advance here is that the team did not simply make another material that absorbs water,” said study co-author Professor Keith Johnston.

“They designed a pathway for water to move quickly, from vapor in the air to liquid on the fiber surface, and then into the interior of the textile.

The researchers are now eyeing applications beyond clothing – including backpacks, tents, emergency shelters and other outdoor gear, allowing items people carry every day to help collect water. They also plan to look at applying the technology to remote field operations, disaster response, and water access in arid or infrastructure-limited regions.

A separate device developed by the same research team pulled a record amount of drinking water from the air using solar power—in both the arid climate of the Chihuahuan Desert and the humidity of Austin, Texas.

In tests, the researchers captured 1.3 liters (2.3 pints) of clean water per day in both locations. That equates to 4.3 liters (7.5 pints) of water per kilo of moisture-capturing materials per day—more than any other research group has achieved, according to a paper published in the journal Nature Water.

“This is a big stride toward practical atmospheric water harvesting,” said study co-lead author Weixin Guan.

OTHER ADVANCEMENTS:
• Ultrasonic Device Dramatically Speeds Harvesting of Water from the Air – Drinkable in Minutes Instead of Hours
• ‘Milking’ the Air for Water: Zero-Energy Technique Doubles Survival Rate for Young Trees to Reforest After Fires
• Device Pulls Dozens of Liters of Water from the Air–Already Being Installed in Jordanian Desert Homes

At the center of the team’s work is AirGel, a specially-engineered hydrogel fabric made from biomass-derived materials. The fabric absorbs moisture from the air, then releases it when warmed.

“This goal has been incubated over years of work, from molecular design to real-world operation, and it is especially meaningful to see those pieces finally come together in a field-ready system,” said Guan.

The University’s research commercialization unit, has filed a patent application for the technology.

Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.

In a public service announcement Thursday, the agencies said water and wastewater utilities have reported incidents to the FBI, with some malicious activity degrading water operations. The announcement does not name the states.

The warning comes after hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water facilities in Minnesota in an attack that had hallmarks of Iranian meddling, according to a law enforcement official. It is still under investigation.

A spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology services agency said Thursday there was no indication the breaches contaminated any municipal water supplies. The federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in a separate alert that some larger attacks on water infrastructure had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” though it did not say where.

Minnesota officials and the U.S. government have not publicly attributed the malicious activity in the state to a specific actor. Likewise, the FBI and the EPA did not identify a culprit behind the breaches in the other states.

President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters Friday at Camp David, blamed Minnesota’s leaders and Gov. Tim Walz, who was the Democratic vice presidential nominee in the 2024 election.

“I think I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” Trump said. “I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘Oh, it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

In response to a request for comment, Walz said in part: “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”

The FBI and EPA advisory focused less on attribution than on the tactics used in the attacks.

The federal advisory said the malicious cyber actors, or MCAs, targeted specific brands of control systems used by municipal water utilities, though the FBI and the EPA urged operators of all systems to take precautions.

Earlier this week, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a bulletin to water contacts in the state, saying  intelligence officials believed that “systems within Wisconsin may be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”

“This leads us to believe that the cyber threat is ongoing in Wisconsin and requires immediate action to prevent potentially serious impacts to our systems,” the bulletin said.

A Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources spokesperson emphasized that intelligence officials in the state “had not yet confirmed that systems in Wisconsin have had connections but are concerned that they might be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”

In the warning, Wisconsin said that Minnesota had reported that hackers managed to drop system pressures, which in “several incidents triggered alarms and prompted a response from law enforcement.”

In an email, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency disputed Wisconsin’s characterizations of the attack and its observed impacts.

“Minnesota has not reported that threat actors lowered pressure across multiple water systems or that pressure changes prompted a law enforcement response,” said the spokesperson, Emily Zimmer.

The agencies said the hackers remotely accessed internet-facing devices, changed IP addresses and passwords, and caused utilities to lose monitoring and control capabilities.

The federal advisory calls on system operators to remove programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, from direct internet exposure by putting them behind secure gateways and firewalls; use strong passwords; and limit communications between authorized control system devices through access control lists.

“Attribution requires careful analysis of technical evidence alongside broader national and international threat intelligence, and our federal partners are best positioned to lead that work,” Zimmer, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency, said.

The breach in Minnesota happened just days after U.S. officials publicly warned that Iran-backed hackers were targeting the nation’s critical infrastructure amid the escalating military conflict between Washington and Tehran.

In a public advisory July 22, CISA, as well as the FBI and other federal agencies, urged companies to boost their defenses, saying Tehran-linked hackers were trying to breach online automated devices used to manage infrastructure systems.

U.S. intelligence agencies have also cautioned that Iran is increasingly able and willing to carry out aggressive cyber operations and that it tried to target water systems in 2023.

Bryson Bort, the founder of the cybersecurity company Scythe and an expert in industrial control system security, said the FBI’s disclosures this week underscore the need for more public awareness of the risks posed by infrastructure breaches.

“We need to be prepared,” Bort said. “Attacks like this illustrate that there are folks who mean the U.S. harm today.”
