Former “American Idol” star and church pastor Caleb Flynn claimed to cops that he “didn’t touch” his wife, whom he’s accused of fatally shooting, according to a recording of his police interview played for jurors Monday before testimony wrapped.

“I’m telling you, I didn’t touch my wife,” Flynn, 40, said as detectives pressed him on whether he gunned down 37-year-old Ashley Flynn inside their Ohio home in February.

“The evidence is a little contrary to that,” one of the investigators responded, according to a report by the Dayton Daily News.

The tape was played before testimony concluded in the case, in which Flynn’s side opted not to call any witnesses. Closing arguments are slated for Tuesday.

The dad of two — who appeared on the competitive singing show in 2013 — is charged with shooting Ashley in the head while she was in bed and as their two daughters, now 10 and 12, slept close by in their rooms.

He then allegedly staged the crime scene at their Tipp City, Ohio house to make it appear like a home invasion.

Prosecutors claimed Flynn’s nearly two-year-long affair with Alleigha Botner, 24, was the motivation behind the killing.

Botner — a fellow worship leader at his church — was one of the 40 witnesses prosecutors called to testify. She was forced to read her own text messages with Flynn saying she wanted to kill his wife.

“It says, ‘I want to kill her, Caleb,'” the ex-mistress said through tears as she read the text exchange to the jury.

“He said, ‘That makes two of us,” Botner said.

“I just wish I didn’t say this,” Botner testified through tears.

Flynn told cops an intruder killed his wife while he was asleep in one of their daughters’ bedrooms. However, investigators testified they never found a shred of evidence to support that claim after a police dog failed to find any scent of an intruder and after cops canvassing the neighborhood failed to turn up any information about the invasion.

His lawyers claimed the prosecution’s case was weak, including the fact that they never recovered the murder weapon. They said the case rested solely on the fact that he had an affair — which wasn’t enough to prove he killed his wife.

Flynn has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder, tampering with evidence and other related crimes. If convicted on the top charge, he faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Amy Tossoun appeared in Mansfield Magistrates' Court today over charges relating to an alleged drink spiking incident at Mount Buller.

The prosecutors and defence lawyers called for a diversion plan to be put in place, but magistrate Amina Bhai said the offences were too serious for a diversion.

The case will return to court in October.

A well-known Melbourne socialite has faced a regional Victorian court charged with spiking a drink at a party at the Mount Buller ski resort.

Amy Tossoun, 34, faced the Mansfield Magistrates' Court today over offences related to an alleged drink spiking in July last year.

She did not enter a plea regarding charges of possessing an amphetamine and introducing a drug of dependence into the body of a person.

Prosecutor Sergeant Karen Knotley told the court that on July 26, 2025, Ms Tossoun and the alleged victim met up with other friends for dinner at the Black Cockatoo restaurant at Mount Buller.

The court heard that after dinner and drinks both groups went to the nearby Kooroora Hotel after 10pm.

Sergeant Knotley told the court the CCTV footage from the club showed that later that evening, Ms Tossoun approached the bar with the alleged victim and another witness.

The alleged victim was hugged by a different person, who turned her away from the bar she was standing at and then was led to a dance floor.

The court heard that CCTV at the club showed Ms Tossoun place the amphetamine into one of the drinks before mixing it with a straw, and then later gave the drink to the alleged victim.

She sipped the drink the accused had given her, thought it tasted strange, then attempted to improve the taste by adding more lime, later asking for more soda to be added.

Later that evening, the alleged victim left the hotel, walked back to their chalet, and started to feel unwell, the court heard.

"She was experiencing extreme dizziness and thought that she was going to faint," Sergeant Knotley told the court.

The court heard the local medical centre was called but there was no answer.

Ambulance paramedics later attended, taking the alleged victim to Mansfield District Hospital in the early hours of July 27.

The alleged victim later tested positive for MDMA, the court heard.

Sergeant Knotley told the court that when Ms Tossoun was interviewed by police, she had a small bag of MDMA in her jacket pocket and said she had placed it in her own drink.

She also told police that the table she was sitting at had a lot of drinks on it, and that if she took the wrong drink the incident was unintentional.

Amy Tossoun appeared in Mansfield Magistrates' Court today. (Instagram: Tanya Mac Creative)

Defence lawyer Michelle Button told the court that the set of circumstances arose in a social setting involving "substances and poor judgement".

She asked magistrate Amina Bhai to afford consideration for diversion.

"The shame and embarrassment of this matter has been significant for [Ms Tossoun]," Ms Button said, citing media attention regarding the case.

"There is a saying … good people make mistakes and bad people do bad things, and this is a set of circumstances where a good person has made a mistake and she's put herself before the court today with the support … of the prosecution and the complainant to seek that Your Honour grant this diversion consideration."

Ms Button told the court that Ms Tossoun had spoken to and texted the alleged victim throughout the night of the incident to ask how she was.

When Magistrate Bhai questioned whether Ms Tossoun told the alleged victim what she had allegedly done on the night, Ms Button told the court that it was not until the next day that those discussions took place, as there was confusion over what had happened.

But she said that in hindsight, Ms Tossoun could have done more during the incident.

The victim allegedly attended a party at the Mount Buller ski resort last year. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

Magistrate Bhai said that while the prosecution and defence both sought diversion, she believed the alleged offences were too serious and there was a need for general deterrence and denouncement.

"You took away the right of another person to say no to consuming a substance, and that being an illicit substance," the magistrate said.

"Not only did you take away her right to say no to that, she didn't know what was happening to her as a result of that.

Ms Button then called for a contest motion, saying she challenged the admissibility of CCTV footage and that she wanted to call several witnesses.

However, Sergeant Knotley told the court the CCTV was very comprehensive.

The matter will return to Mansfield Magistrates' Court in October.

By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

The Coalition has floated new ideas that could allow Australians to use their retirement savings to buy a home, reigniting debate about the role of superannuation in housing.

Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg is due to argue in an address on Tuesday that the country must rethink the role superannuation could play in boosting home ownership as the number of retirees renting continues to rise.

While not official Coalition policy, he said the party wants to explore whether Australians should be given more freedom to use their own savings to secure housing earlier in life.

'We want to have a country where more people are retired home owners,' he told ABC News Radio on Tuesday morning.

'One of the most worrying trends we have is the growth in retired renters.'

Ideas under consideration include allowing super balances to be used as collateral for a mortgage, offsetting home loans with retirement savings, or letting people withdraw funds to buy a first home or reduce existing mortgage debt.

'There are a whole range of different ways you could do it,' Bragg added.

'You could keep the money in the system and it could operate as collateral or an offset. You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first-home loan.'

Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg (pictured) warned that a rising number of retirees are now renting rather than owning their homes

The Coalition previously proposed letting first-home buyers withdraw up to $50,000 from their super to purchase property, but abandoned the policy after the 2022 election loss.

Bragg insisted he is not backing a specific model, but wants to spark a wider discussion about how housing and retirement policy interact.

'Today's address is about setting out the rationale for having a more sophisticated debate,' he said.

'I'm not advocating any particular solutions today, but I think it's important that we look to ensure that we do all we can to drive up home ownership rates.'

Bragg pointed to data showing many Australians already use superannuation to eliminate housing debt later in life.

According to Bragg, 32 per cent of lump-sum super withdrawals are used to pay off mortgages once people reach preservation age.

'We now have 32 per cent of lump sums out of super being used to pay off mortgages at preservation age, which is 60,' he said.

'Surely it's worth us looking at whether you could effectively calibrate that earlier.'

Treasurer Jim Chalmers quickly dismissed Bragg's pitch, accusing the Coalition of again targeting Australia's retirement savings

He argued that reducing mortgage debt sooner could save households significant interest charges and make it more likely people enter retirement as home owners.

Bragg also framed the issue as part of broader challenges set out in the Intergenerational Report, which highlights shifting demographics and renewed focus on retirement outcomes.

'The important point here is that we believe that home ownership is the bedrock of your retirement,' Bragg said.

'In fact, it is the key determinant of your success in retirement.'

The idea has faced strong resistance from Labor and the super industry who argue early access to super undermines the system's purpose and weakens compound returns.

Critics also warn such policies could drive up house prices by boosting borrowing power without addressing the housing shortage.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers dismissed the proposal, accusing the Coalition of once again targeting Australians' retirement savings.

'Well, they hate super. They always have, and they always will,' Chalmers told ABC News Radio.

Anthony Albanese (pictured) was slammed over declaring super a 'national asset' in July

'They're coming after superannuation, and they put all of their time and effort into copying One Nation on superannuation; that would be devastating for people's retirement incomes.'

Chalmers argued the government's latest Intergenerational Report showed the need to protect super for retirement, not use it as a band-aid for housing affordability.

'The intergenerational report makes it really clear just how important that is to the future of our country, the economy, retirement incomes, and budget pressures.'

The Coalition has previously accused Chalmers of seeking to steer Australians' retirement savings towards government-backed priorities after Labor figures described the nation's $4trillion-plus superannuation pool as a 'national asset'.

Opposition figures have argued superannuation should be managed solely in members' interests rather than directed towards government objectives, while also criticising the links between industry super funds and unions as major donors to the Labor Party.

The Coalition's push follows a One Nation proposal that would allow renters and mortgage holders to redirect part of their compulsory super contributions into their take-home pay for up to three years.

Under the plan, 3 per cent of a worker's super contribution would be paid directly to them instead of remaining in their retirement account.

Hanson said the policy would have a 'neutral' effect on inflation and give households extra 'breathing room'.

'For a working couple earning $168,000 between them, it is about $4,300 a year after tax, or $82 a week, back in the family budget,' she said.

Business leaders have previously cautioned against greater government involvement in the sector.

In July, Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller urged Canberra to leave the system alone.

'Don't touch the super complex, don't direct it, don't tell it where to go,' he said.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently been discussing “artificial general intelligence” that matches or surpasses human capabilities. This is from the same person who has said children born today (including his own) will “never be more intelligent than AI, from a ‘raw IQ’” (intelligence quotient) perspective.

One lucky Tyee reader will receive a family pack of tickets to The Cultch’s annual holiday production, plus a gift card to Bombay Kitchen.

United States President Donald Trump has also recently mused about who is and who is not “high IQ.”

As a scholar rooted in the history of Canadian higher education and its intersections with rhetoric around disability and race, every time I hear the word “intelligence,” including as “IQ,” I get jumpy.

“Intelligence” clearly has a high-stakes and worrisome future, but also a dark history.

To figure out what AI might be replacing, we need to better understand intelligence as a historically situated idea — and a dangerous one — rather than as some sort of biological fact.

For universities, this reflection matters as institutions confront questions about how their responses to AI align with their missions.

‘Intelligence’ and eugenics

In the early 20th century, universities, university disciplines and academic careers were built by crafting scientific-sounding definitions and measures of “intelligence” and “IQ.”

As historian Gerald Thompson  notes, the creator and head of the University of Toronto’s department of educational research, Peter Sandiford, tested the “intelligence” of Chinese and Japanese Canadian students in British Columbia in the 1920s.

This was done under the direction of the first full professor of education at the University of British Columbia, George Moir Weir.

The research, writes Thompson, “was meant to confirm” long-standing racist notions of Anglo-white superiority and Asian inferiority.

As historians like Angus McLaren have demonstrated, such projects were the work of eugenics. These defined intelligence as a genetic and inheritable trait that could be measured but not necessarily easily developed within individuals, and assumed a pseudo-scientific racialized genetic hierarchy.

Eugenic ideas of intelligence shaped residential schools

Researchers involved in such projects ranked Canadians, and these rankings determined educational and social futures. Eugenic ideas of intelligence deeply shaped residential schools and their colonial legacies.

Sociologist Alexandra Giancarlo has documented how in the 1930s, Kenneth E. Kidd, who went on to found the “Indian-Eskimo Studies” program at Trent University, administered a series of IQ tests at the Mohawk Institute, a residential school in southern Ontario.

This led to two published books that advanced racist ideas around intelligence and informed Department of Indian Affairs policy not just for children at the Mohawk Institute, but at residential schools across the country.

Some of the researchers — such as Weir, Kidd and Sandiford, who contributed to popularizing these ideas — went on to build university programs and disciplines.

The more general result was that universities and academics claimed a major stake as measurers of intelligence. This coincided with an increased reliance on testing, exams and grading at Canadian universities and academic rankings.

Now, because of the fear of AI cheating, educators are grappling with forms of assessment. In some cases, this means more hand-written or oral exams, which raise concerns about ableism.

In the past, measuring intelligence was a way to exclude entire groups of people from opportunity. How will intelligence be used and misused going forward?

Teaching, learning and AI

These histories influence how we talk about artificial intelligence, and should also shape how we position teaching and learning today.

The intersection of AI and eugenics is beginning to be studied more deeply, for instance by the Rutgers AI Lab. The lab notes this technology may be “shaping people to fit a narrow standard of intelligence, health, ability or social worth” often “through data, algorithms, or evaluation systems that encode biased ideas about who has potential and who does not.”

Likewise, the impacts of AI usage on learning and “de-skilling” have been extensively explored, with some people calling de-skilling “enfeeblement,” perhaps unaware of the eugenic history of this wording: “feeble-mindedness” was a  pseudoscientific, eugenic term.

As disability studies scholar Rua Williams argues, “through ignorance of the historical context,” the current project of artificial intelligence may be “replicating historical and political projects that devalue human beings on the basis of abstract or fabricated concepts” of intelligence.

Others express concern that a lack of regulation around AI is coinciding with authoritarian politics and ideas.

What is the role for education and educators?

On the one hand, we are told that technology is already “smarter” than we are, smarter than we can teach our young people to be. On the other hand, we are asked trust people like Altman to train or regulate this AI.

What role is there, then, for education and educators?

Reflecting on the history of IQ testing should prompt universities to call into question the value that we have placed on IQ to begin with.

IQ was at first an educational tool; it was gradually transformed into a weapon used to identify and segregate whole populations based on terrible science.

Educators will need to confront how many of the ways that we have built efficiency and credibility have also sought to validate our expertise in testing and ranking, sometimes understood as quantifying intelligence.

Ironically, our institutions’ obsessions with standardizing education and their over-emphasis on grading and assessing students has made our work too easy to automate.

It has also arguably contributed to grade inflation and other trends that devalue our important work.

What to do? Focus on connection, critical thinking

So, what do educators do? We should focus, more than ever, on the collaboration and critical thinking our students do, as well as how they connect through relationships and learn to connect ideas. We should move away from high-stakes testing, measuring and grading.

“Intelligence” itself has been an ableist, even eugenic, construct — certainly in how and why it has been measured.

Teaching and learning in contemporary universities can be much more dynamic, interpersonal and human. Our innovative classroom practices can lead other educators to resist transactional teaching as well.

We need to continue asking: “What is intelligence?” And we need to provide different answers to this question than we ever have throughout the history of higher education.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently been discussing “artificial general intelligence” that matches or surpasses human capabilities. This is from the same person who has said children born today (including his own) will “never be more intelligent than AI, from a ‘raw IQ’” (intelligence quotient) perspective.

One lucky Tyee reader will receive a family pack of tickets to The Cultch’s annual holiday production, plus a gift card to Bombay Kitchen.

United States President Donald Trump has also recently mused about who is and who is not “high IQ.”

As a scholar rooted in the history of Canadian higher education and its intersections with rhetoric around disability and race, every time I hear the word “intelligence,” including as “IQ,” I get jumpy.

“Intelligence” clearly has a high-stakes and worrisome future, but also a dark history.

To figure out what AI might be replacing, we need to better understand intelligence as a historically situated idea — and a dangerous one — rather than as some sort of biological fact.

For universities, this reflection matters as institutions confront questions about how their responses to AI align with their missions.

‘Intelligence’ and eugenics

In the early 20th century, universities, university disciplines and academic careers were built by crafting scientific-sounding definitions and measures of “intelligence” and “IQ.”

As historian Gerald Thompson  notes, the creator and head of the University of Toronto’s department of educational research, Peter Sandiford, tested the “intelligence” of Chinese and Japanese Canadian students in British Columbia in the 1920s.

This was done under the direction of the first full professor of education at the University of British Columbia, George Moir Weir.

The research, writes Thompson, “was meant to confirm” long-standing racist notions of Anglo-white superiority and Asian inferiority.

As historians like Angus McLaren have demonstrated, such projects were the work of eugenics. These defined intelligence as a genetic and inheritable trait that could be measured but not necessarily easily developed within individuals, and assumed a pseudo-scientific racialized genetic hierarchy.

Eugenic ideas of intelligence shaped residential schools

Researchers involved in such projects ranked Canadians, and these rankings determined educational and social futures. Eugenic ideas of intelligence deeply shaped residential schools and their colonial legacies.

Sociologist Alexandra Giancarlo has documented how in the 1930s, Kenneth E. Kidd, who went on to found the “Indian-Eskimo Studies” program at Trent University, administered a series of IQ tests at the Mohawk Institute, a residential school in southern Ontario.

This led to two published books that advanced racist ideas around intelligence and informed Department of Indian Affairs policy not just for children at the Mohawk Institute, but at residential schools across the country.

Some of the researchers — such as Weir, Kidd and Sandiford, who contributed to popularizing these ideas — went on to build university programs and disciplines.

The more general result was that universities and academics claimed a major stake as measurers of intelligence. This coincided with an increased reliance on testing, exams and grading at Canadian universities and academic rankings.

Now, because of the fear of AI cheating, educators are grappling with forms of assessment. In some cases, this means more hand-written or oral exams, which raise concerns about ableism.

In the past, measuring intelligence was a way to exclude entire groups of people from opportunity. How will intelligence be used and misused going forward?

Teaching, learning and AI

These histories influence how we talk about artificial intelligence, and should also shape how we position teaching and learning today.

The intersection of AI and eugenics is beginning to be studied more deeply, for instance by the Rutgers AI Lab. The lab notes this technology may be “shaping people to fit a narrow standard of intelligence, health, ability or social worth” often “through data, algorithms, or evaluation systems that encode biased ideas about who has potential and who does not.”

Likewise, the impacts of AI usage on learning and “de-skilling” have been extensively explored, with some people calling de-skilling “enfeeblement,” perhaps unaware of the eugenic history of this wording: “feeble-mindedness” was a  pseudoscientific, eugenic term.

As disability studies scholar Rua Williams argues, “through ignorance of the historical context,” the current project of artificial intelligence may be “replicating historical and political projects that devalue human beings on the basis of abstract or fabricated concepts” of intelligence.

Others express concern that a lack of regulation around AI is coinciding with authoritarian politics and ideas.

What is the role for education and educators?

On the one hand, we are told that technology is already “smarter” than we are, smarter than we can teach our young people to be. On the other hand, we are asked trust people like Altman to train or regulate this AI.

What role is there, then, for education and educators?

Reflecting on the history of IQ testing should prompt universities to call into question the value that we have placed on IQ to begin with.

IQ was at first an educational tool; it was gradually transformed into a weapon used to identify and segregate whole populations based on terrible science.

Educators will need to confront how many of the ways that we have built efficiency and credibility have also sought to validate our expertise in testing and ranking, sometimes understood as quantifying intelligence.

Ironically, our institutions’ obsessions with standardizing education and their over-emphasis on grading and assessing students has made our work too easy to automate.

It has also arguably contributed to grade inflation and other trends that devalue our important work.

What to do? Focus on connection, critical thinking

So, what do educators do? We should focus, more than ever, on the collaboration and critical thinking our students do, as well as how they connect through relationships and learn to connect ideas. We should move away from high-stakes testing, measuring and grading.

“Intelligence” itself has been an ableist, even eugenic, construct — certainly in how and why it has been measured.

Teaching and learning in contemporary universities can be much more dynamic, interpersonal and human. Our innovative classroom practices can lead other educators to resist transactional teaching as well.

We need to continue asking: “What is intelligence?” And we need to provide different answers to this question than we ever have throughout the history of higher education.

A non-surgical knee procedure provided yearlong pain relief for 80% of patients in a new study. The treatment reduces inflammation without permanent implants, but researchers note important limitations.

A non-surgical procedure that temporarily blocks extra blood vessels in the knee is offering lasting pain relief for people with knee osteoarthritis.

In a clinical study of 194 patients, 80% of them reported significant reductions in knee pain that lasted for at least a full year after receiving the treatment.

The findings highlight a potential alternative for millions of adults with chronic joint pain who have outgrown pain medications or steroid injections — but who want to avoid total knee replacement.

WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF

Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and causes the body to grow unnecessary new blood vessels around the knee, according to Mayo Clinic.

These extra vessels increase inflammation and irritate surrounding nerves, making daily movement painful.

Up to 80% of knee osteoarthritis patients in a new study experienced clinically meaningful, long-term pain reduction lasting at least one full year. (iStock)

The procedure, known as genicular artery embolization (GAE), addresses this directly.

By temporarily clogging excess blood vessels, doctors can reduce inflammation and quiet pain-sensing nerves without major surgery or permanent implants.

Because the treatment uses microscopic gelatin particles that dissolve over time, it leaves no foreign material behind. If widely adopted, GAE could provide a repeatable, low-risk way for patients to stay active and preserve joint function longer, researchers say.

"We saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function."

"For many patients with knee osteoarthritis, there is a real treatment gap today," said Florian Nima Fleckenstein, M.D., deputy head of Interventional Radiology Campus Mitte, Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin, in a press release.

"Our study demonstrates that GAE using rapidly resorbable gelatin-based microspheres is a safe, minimally invasive therapy that provides meaningful pain relief and functional improvement in participants with osteoarthritis-related knee symptoms for at least 12 months."

ALZHEIMER’S RISK LINKED TO COMPOUND FOUND IN POPULAR JOINT HEALTH SUPPLEMENTS

During GAE, doctors use real-time X-ray guidance to steer a thin, flexible tube into the blood vessels surrounding the knee joint.

Then they release tiny, dissolvable gelatin particles into specific vessels to slow excess blood flow to the inflamed areas.

Unlike traditional joint implants, the microscopic gelatin particles dissolve naturally over time after calming local inflammation. (iStock)

Across 239 total procedures performed on 194 study participants, none experienced severe complications.

Only 6.7% reported mild side effects, such as brief skin discoloration or minor bruising, issues that resolved on their own.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"In our cohort, we saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function, including sports and recreation and daily activity," Fleckenstein said.

"Most importantly, their quality of life significantly increased."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

In addition to feeling less pain, participants experienced gains in daily mobility. Patients reported easier walking, climbing stairs and bending, while overall quality-of-life scores more than doubled over the 12-month follow-up period.

While the results are promising, researchers note several important limitations.

First, the study did not include a control group receiving a mock or placebo procedure.

Because the study on knee pain lacked a placebo control group and tracked outcomes for only 12 months, larger randomized trials are needed to confirm the long-term duration and physiological impact of the new treatment. (iStock)

Without a comparison group, it is difficult to isolate the physical benefits of the dissolvable particles from potential placebo effects, the researchers said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Second, the study tracked patients for only one year.

Further research is needed to determine how long the pain relief typically lasts and how often repeat treatments might be required.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Finally, while GAE effectively reduces inflammation and pain, the researchers said it is not a cure.

The procedure does not rebuild lost cartilage or reverse structural joint damage. Larger, randomized trials are currently underway to confirm these early findings.

Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors for further comment.

Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.

The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.

"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.

"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."

Sam Wright took over as head coach at the end of 2023 and has struggled to get wins on the board since. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.

"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.

"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.

"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."

Ruby Schleicher, captain of Collingwood, will leave the Magpies at the end of the AFLW season. (Getty: Martin Keep)

Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.

Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.

He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.

Former player and coach Lauren Arnell slams non-offensive styles of play in the AFLW. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.

"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.

"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."

Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.

Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.

Essendon players have looked frustrated and dejected after losses this season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.

There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.

On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.

"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

A federal appeals court ruled Friday that illegal immigrants detained inside the United States have no constitutional right to a bond hearing, no matter how long they have lived in the country.

A bond hearing allows detained migrants to ask an immigration judge for release on bond while their immigration cases proceed.

In a 10-7 decision, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans reversed a lower panel and sided with the Trump administration. The ruling closed the main legal route that judges in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi had used to free detained migrants who challenged how long they were being held.

The ruling backs a policy, put in place last year, that lets the government hold immigrants arrested in the interior until their deportation cases end, without giving them a chance to argue for release before a judge. It is a sharp break from how previous administrations handled such cases, when migrants who were not flight risks or dangers could often post bond.

Writing for the majority, Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, said the men challenging their detention were still legally seeking admission to the country and were not entitled to a hearing on due-process grounds. The judge wrote that they could end their confinement “at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”

The three men at the center of the case came from Mexico and Honduras, have U.S.-citizen children, and were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traffic stops. One of them had lived in the United States for more than 22 years.

In a concurring opinion, Judge James Ho said the court was defending basic national authority. “A nation ceases to be a nation if it can’t protect its borders,” he wrote, adding that the dissenting judges would hand illegal immigrants an incentive to settle in the country unlawfully.

The dissenters argued that the decision cut long-term residents off from constitutional protections the Supreme Court has long recognized.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, called the decision a “big win” on social media.

The ruling comes weeks after the Supreme Court agreed to take up a related case on the same detention policy. The justices, however, are weighing only whether federal immigration law requires bond hearings, not whether the Constitution does — the question the Fifth Circuit answered Friday.
